Upper limits on the amount of magic needed to run quantum circuits can be found by using measures like depth and width in addition to size. A recent study improves the state of knowledge by setting the width-based limit to O(log d) and the combined depth and width limit to O(log^2 d), both improving previous results.

This research investigates the behavior of the universe by applying holographic dark energy in conjunction with a non-extensive entropy formula, and we demonstrate that, when utilizing the Essence model, our theoretical framework is capable of reconciling the universe's accelerated expansion with its previous phases of expansion.

Between 2018 and 2019, four $K$2 plates were subjected to an on-sky test using the 3.5-meter optical telescope. Utilizing a 1-degree field-of-view, multi-object fiber spectrograph, we gathered a wealth of data on stellar spectra. With an efficient system, around 3000 stars were observed per exposure, and approximately 3000 valid exposures with overlapping fields yielded around 9 million spectra. Our analysis focused on four notable stars, and we successfully obtained high-quality spectra for each. Furthermore, we developed a high-performance algorithm for matching spectra, and we demonstrated its efficacy through successful cross-identification of the four plates, resulting in around 1.5 million spectra matches. Our research suggests a potential for the $\mathit{LAMOST}$ $\mathit{SkySurvey}$ to contribute valuable data to various fields of astronomy, and we have developed a data release that will be further expanded upon completion of the $\mathit{SkySurvey}$.

This paper proposes an innovative method for generating genuine random numbers in embedded systems, combining a simplified approach with high performance. It leverages the properties of an SRAM-based True Random Number Creator (TRNC) to create randomness from memory initialization errors in the soft-core processor it is integrated with. The SRAM is reconfigured as a linear feedback shift register (LFSR) to produce an erratic output. Performance evaluations using a Xilinx Vivado platform reveal that the TRNC is both cost-effective and efficient. It is compatible with existing hardware and can be easily implemented in the processor's hardware for real-time number creation.

This research explores the concept of single-electron resistor switches based on molecules, which have not been thoroughly examined in previous studies. In our simulations, we found that certain types of molecules, particularly those consisting of a single atom, are ideal for Thiele-effect single-electron resistor switches, which have been made operational in our experiments. Our findings indicate that broadening the range of suitable molecules is crucial, and therefore, we propose considering multi-atomic linear molecules, which have also shown exceptional performance in recently achieved double single-electron transistors.

The visualization of complex loop calculations in quantum field theory is examined, particularly for higher-order and loop-carrying integrals and their derivatives with respect to spacetime position. The FeynmanDiagramAlgebra package in Mathematica is employed to derive key relationships between these objects and determine their values based on specific numerical evaluations. This study extends previous work on two-point functions by considering more general cases, such as space-time indices and external derivatives. The findings are further elaborated through supplementary mathematical expressions presented in the accompanying material.

We analyze and solve the time-space evolution equations for one-dimensional, two-state quantum walks via an eigenfunction expansion method. This approach also yields a set of ordinary differential equations that can define the time-space evolution, which we find aligns with existing known results. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the expansion coefficients' initial values and the wavefunction's initial values.

This study investigates the composition of hybrid stars, consisting of a quark core surrounded by nuclear matter, by combining the Sigma-omega-rho model with the MIT and NJL models. By combining these models, we are able to describe the transition between quark and nuclear matter. Utilizing the combined Sigma-omega-rho-QMC model, we examine the mass-radius relationship of hybrid stars with varying core pressures, and determine the maximum mass of such stars. Subsequently, the results are compared to observational data, and the mass-radius relationship of a $1.4 M_{\odot}$ star is analyzed. Furthermore, the composition of the core in such a star is discussed.

$q$-deformation, initially developed in theoretical physics to describe noncommutative systems and particle statistics, has been successfully applied to various fields such as quantum field theory, string theory, and optomechanics. In this context, we explore the impact of $q$-deformation on optomechanics by incorporating a driven $q$-deformed optomechanical system into an external drive. We analyze the $q$-deformed Fock state density matrix and examine its effective nonlinearity, particularly in the context of optomechanical transparency. Our findings reveal that $q$-deformation enhances the nonlinearity in optomechanics, thereby improving the interaction between optical and mechanical components. Furthermore, $q$-deformation offers a means to manipulate the optical carrier frequency and Raman process. Notably, choosing an appropriate $q$ value can eliminate optomechanical transparency, while specific $q$ values can amplify the optical signal by up to 1000%. Additionally, $q$-deformation enables the realization of optomechanical transparency at both the optical and mechanical frequencies, thus broadening the possibilities for optomechanical applications.

A rarer type of R-parity broken mode has been discovered, which arises when two distinct types of rotational motion interact, specifically an intrinsic motion and a deformation in the R-condensate. Using a simplified model that treats the system as two rotating parts, researchers found that the conditions necessary for these adverse R-parity broken states to occur can be mapped out by mapping the parameters of Normal R-parity broken states in a similar way. Further examination of the scissors modes within this model revealed that the characteristics associated with the intrinsic angular momentum, including its magnitude and relationship to other components, can be accurately predicted. These findings align well with observations made through experimental data analysis.

Our research focuses on ultrathin films made of transition metal atoms, specifically those that are just a few atoms thick and grown on top of a substrate. These films exhibit various types of magnetic properties, and our focus is on those that are only one atom thick versus those that are two atoms thick. This comparison between the two types of films reveals significant differences in their magnetic behavior due to the distinct ways in which the atoms are arranged and interact with each other. By studying this contrast, we gain valuable insights into the fundamental magnetic properties of these materials, which can be compared to their bulk counterparts. This analysis helps us better understand the relationship between spin and orbital fluctuations and how they evolve under different levels of dimensionality.

We've conducted both numerical and analytical research into the equilibrium properties of laser-cooled atoms in a heated environment, finding that temperature cooling has a limiting effect and the equilibrium distribution is, in fact, broader than the Maxwellian. The magnitude and shape of this distribution are influenced by the equilibrium's temperature. We discovered that this unusual behavior persists across all temperatures and can be understood through the generalized Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem. Furthermore, this phenomenon isn't an exception but rather the norm in systems subjected to a coolizing force.

This study examines a cryptocurrency trading network through multiple lenses, 
utilizing network science and mutual information theory. Firstly, it identifies 
significant pairs of cryptocurrencies based on their linear and nonlinear co-movements, 
revealing a prevalent correlation between Bitcoin and Ethereum trading volumes. 
Furthermore, it constructs a corresponding graph and analyzes its structural 
properties, revealing prevalent motifs such as "hubs" - entities with extensive 
connections - located in the network's central region. Secondly, it employs principal 
component analysis to uncover concurrent trends among large groups of cryptocurrencies, 
demonstrating persistent correlations across multiple time periods and highlighting 
a consistent correlation between Ethereum's price and trading volume.

A thorough investigation of the effects of zero-point motion on the properties of tiny molecular clusters of H2SO4 and H2O has been conducted, using a combination of high-level ab initio calculations and statistical sampling methods. The importance of these effects is particularly pronounced in such small systems, where they can shift the equilibrium temperature and affect the accuracy of thermodynamic predictions derived from the canonical thermodynamics. To accurately model the vibrational states of these clusters, a transition from harmonic to anharmonic treatment is required, and our findings indicate that anharmonic behavior is already evident in 10-particle systems. These effects are examined through the development of a custom code that combines a high-level potential energy surface with molecular dynamics simulations, and our findings demonstrate that the canonical approach underestimates the temperature at which the clusters react. Furthermore, the application of this method to unassociated 5-water clusters reveals the presence of significant anharmonicity, as well as the emergence of roton features in the phonon spectrum, signaling the onset of pre-iceberg crystallization.

We establish the topological structure of a specific subset within the space of partial isometries in finite dimensional vector spaces, given that perception pairs and equivariant spaces are involved, and we demonstrate its relationship to the space of group isometries, and finally, we show that it is compact and Hausdorff when a certain topological property is inherited.

In one-dimensional systems with non-geometric memory, we have discovered a system-wide response phenomenon, similar to mechanical and electrical reactions, that occurs in half of the system. This reaction behavior is found at a specific point in time and frequency and arises due to the absence of equilibrium and the presence of topological properties that protect it. The time it takes for this reaction to occur is directly related to how the system's excitation spectrum is shifted from equilibrium. The feature of not having an energy gap in the excitation spectrum causes the reaction time to be infinitely long when the system reaches equilibrium.

This study delves into a fundamental question in machine learning - the structure of models trained using neural networks, specifically focusing on why they tend to have simple characteristics. We show that the successful simplification of models can be attributed to a combination of statistical properties and the inherent features of data, rather than just their underlying geometry. Our analysis also reveals that certain characteristics of data can be stabilizing for simple models, and we explore how the complexity of data affects the interaction between models' simplicity and their performance.

Our research provides an in-depth examination of angular distribution properties in $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, with a focus on standard model predictions. We explore how various Wilson coefficients influence these distributions, considering both individual changes and combinations of multiple coefficients. This comprehensive analysis serves as a useful reference for interpreting experimental data and extracting Wilson coefficients, leveraging the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay channel.

Automated essay scoring using machine learning models is an effective approach, 
yet the scarcity of labeled data poses a significant challenge for training robust models. 
This study focuses on enhancing the performance of automated essay scoring models, 
specifically those employing Transformer-based architectures, to overcome data limitations. 
To achieve this, we developed a novel data augmentation method that leverages a pre-trained 
Transformer model to generate "soft" transformations of existing essays. 
By utilizing a small margin from the original essay, we ensure that the generated variations 
retain their original meaning, thereby avoiding the pitfalls of hard data augmentation techniques. 
Our approach was implemented and tested on the 2018 SAT essay dataset, 
demonstrating that the use of soft data augmentation significantly improves scoring accuracy.

Early 20th-century interest in financial risk is exemplified by the famous quote from John Maynard Keynes: "A rise in the price of bullion could be triggered by the emperors of Rome wearing red instead of black." This underscores the importance of understanding and predicting subtle connections between seemingly unrelated factors.

This research project examines how skill distribution evolves across generations, 
taking into account the dynamic nature of mobility between different social groups. 
We're developing a model that uses a mean-field approach to study the distribution of opportunities 
across generations, taking into account stochastic fluctuations. Analytical solutions for steady-state 
scenarios with and without intergroup marriage are obtained, revealing how different parameters affect 
the distribution of skills and opportunities. Our analysis reveals that in the absence of intergroup marriage, 
the distribution of opportunities remains largely stable across generations, 
regardless of the initial distribution. However, introducing marriages between generations can lead to 
gradual changes in the distribution, taking into account the mobility rates within different social groups. 
Our findings have implications for policy-making, particularly in the context of equal opportunity policies. 
We discuss how such policies can be implemented to promote greater equity in the distribution of skills and opportunities.

The link between a particle's spin and its statistics, which is not directly related to relativity, is better understood through a fundamental connection that ties non-relativistic exchange symmetry to spatial coordinate parity. We demonstrate that exchanging two identical bosons with an even number of spatial components and fermons with an odd number preserves parity, while not consistently doing so for particles with intermediate spins.

Delegated RingCT is an enhanced version of RingCT, featuring a simplified verification process.
The ring signature, a key component of RingCT, involves multiple key generation steps, resulting in relatively complex verification.
To address this issue, Delegated RingCT simplifies RingCT by substituting the sign-verify process with a BLS sign-verify protocol.
By leveraging the properties of bilinear pairings, BLS sign-verifiable protocol achieves signature aggregation, thus reducing verification time.
As a result, verification in Delegated RingCT is significantly faster than RingCT, while maintaining the same level of security.

This study investigates the difficulty of solving linear systems where matrices have a specific pattern, characterized by a combination of non-zero and zero entries. We focus on matrices that can be categorized as D-sparse, meaning they have a certain level of sparsity. A novel concept, space toughness, is introduced to assess the minimum memory required by a randomized algorithm to determine if a given matrix belongs to a specific set. Our analysis reveals that for a wide range of sparsity levels, there is a significant gap between the memory needed by the most efficient known algorithms and our established lower bound. Additionally, we show it is challenging to create efficient algorithms that can verify the properties of a matrix with a specific structure within a smaller amount of memory.

Massive vector boson creation is a rare phenomenon that serves as a sensitive test of the Standard Model in its non-perturbative aspects. This study presents the first experimental findings on the simultaneous production of three massive gauge bosos at 13 TeV for the LHC, utilizing the CMS detector using 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at 13 TeV. This sample was analyzed to identify events featuring three lepton jets and large missing energy levels. This analysis led to upper limits on cross-sections being set for various combinations of gauge boson types, with some being measured and others being theory-based predictions. These findings were found to be in line with predictions from the Standard Model, with a significance of 1.1 sigma. This study was found to possess a potential sensitivity of 0.41 fb for a particular combination of specific gauge bosons at a 5 sigma level of significance, with a potential future sensitivity of 0.13 fb at 350 fb$^{-1}$ of accumulated data.

Hebrew possesses rich morphological characteristics, making it challenging to
automatically parse. We have undertaken the full text mining pipeline for a
corpus of 1.1 million tokens from the Jerusalem Post, 2006 - 2012. This involves
creating a high-quality tagger and parser using transfer learning and
fine-tuning approaches. Our results show that we have achieved near-state-of-the-art
accuracy in tagging tasks, while also achieving significant improvements in parsing
F1 scores across multiple evaluation scenarios. Our study demonstrates the
feasibility of generating a large corpus of automatically tagged and parsed
Hebrew text using transfer learning and fine-tuning techniques.

This article demonstrates that most subsets of the l_p space maintain their inherent compressibility when transformed into smaller subsets. Specifically, it is proven that these subsets significantly reduce dimension only if they are essentially one-dimensional. The findings are based on the epsilon-isometric dimension decrease theorem, which is a new and innovative concept in this context.

Over the past few decades, there has been a notable increase in scientific data availability, which has outpaced the capacity of individual researchers to manage and analyze them. This surge in data presents an opportunity to harness the power of multiple contributors to achieve significant scientific breakthroughs. This paper outlines the theoretical framework for one type of interdependent relationship, where numerous agents cooperatively gather extensive datasets to feed into complex simulation models. This relationship is prevalent in various fields, including the study of celestial bodies, disease spread, and high-energy physics. We have developed and tested a series of procedures to facilitate this type of collaboration, which includes the development of a data exchange protocol, the creation of a centralized database, and a system for evaluating the impact of different model variations. An example of our methodology in action is the analysis of up to 100,000 images of distant galaxies, which was made possible through a substantial collaboration involving over 1,000 scientists.

Current research has limited success in mitigating the adverse effects of degree distribution correlations within low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. We analyze the performance of LDPC codes with deleted bits in terms of both average and higher-order moment correlations between degree distributions. Our findings reveal significant impacts of degree-degree correlations on thresholding and error floors. We derive an approximate expression for the threshold of such codes, which aligns well with simulations. We also develop an outer bound on the minimum distance of these codes, which converges to the binary erasure channel (BEC) LDPC code bound as higher moment correlations approach zero. Notably, certain degree-degree correlations can yield better minimum distances than randomly constructed BECDs. We provide a novel LDPC code with finite length and demonstrate its resilience, 5 times greater, compared to an LDPC code with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) degrees.

This research proposes a predictive synthesis method for generating a secure filter that can be applied to any system, regardless of its individual components. The proposed filter synthesizer is capable of creating a closed-loop system with guaranteed stability and performance within specified bounds. The synthesis of the predictive secure filter is based on an model that is derived from the system's real-time operational data. The root of this method lies in formulating an secure control problem that ensures intervention only when and to the extent necessary to maintain system safety. The resulting predictive secure filter can be implemented in two modes: either in a hardware in the loop setup or in software, providing real-time protection for the system it is integrated with.

We're investigating the security implications of allocating a quantum key using the phase-randomized cat state method. Our analysis centers on a scenario where the sender randomly alters the phase in half of the cat states after preparing a block, and the receiver changes the corresponding basis in the matching recipient addresses. The results indicate that security can still be confirmed under these conditions due to the receiver's ability to accurately identify the phase in approximately half of the cases. However, if the sender alters the phase in more than 50% of instances, the key allocation process is compromised as the key rate becomes vulnerable to manipulation by eavesdroppers.

This study examines how a large-scale language model's pretraining influences its ability to learn new tasks in the context of its existing knowledge. For a range of benchmark tasks, researchers found that modifying the initial pretraining corpus can significantly alter the model's performance both before and after subsequent learning. Furthermore, they discovered that certain characteristics of the pretraining corpus, specifically its length and writing style, have a substantial impact on the model's ability to learn in the context. It's important to note that this investigation centers solely on the model's pretraining, disregarding any subsequent learning it undergoes.

We investigated the development of galaxies within the Centaurus cluster, specifically focusing on the interaction between the hot intracluster medium and the surrounding cold clouds. To do this, we employed a 2D simulation that varied the influence of radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and the transfer of heat. Our results revealed that the collapse of the cold clouds primarily occurred through a process known as the Rayleigh-Taylor instability, with the addition of a vertical heat transfer mechanism accelerating this process. However, magnetic fields with a turbulent energy cascade capable of transferring energy to smaller scales significantly slowed the collapse, with the strength of the magnetic field and the ratio of specific heat capacities determining the type of collapse. Furthermore, the interaction between the clouds and the hot intracluster medium led to the growth of the cold clouds through thermal instabilities, with magnetic fields again playing a crucial role in the process.

This study investigates the concept of CP violation in the context of semileptonic decays. We have established a relationship between various branching ratios, which allows for the identification of cases where final state particles can be distinguished. Specifically, we examine the elegance and aesthetic appeal of these distinctions. By analyzing the elegance of CP-conjugate processes based on differing numbers of leptons and antileptons in the final state, a connection with Fermi-Dirac statistics emerges. Moreover, we explore how the elegance of these distinctions correlates with other semileptonic decay modes.

In superstring theory, data on hard string scattering has been scarce due to a lack of relevant amplitude data. Recent breakthroughs, however, have yielded significant results, particularly concerning the behavior of scattering amplitudes in the context of dual resonance models. A newly discovered pattern, $\mathcal{A}(s,t,u) \sim \frac{1}{st} + \frac{1}{su} + \frac{1}{tu}$, has been found, and it contradicts the long-held Gross conjecture. This outcome has far-reaching implications, especially in relation to the AdS/CFT correspondence and the unification of gravity and gauge interactions. These findings also align with the expectations of the Swampland program, including the Weak Gravity Conjecture.

As the core network forms an essential framework for a wireless communication system, its optimized design directly impacts the overall performance of the entire system. With 5G technology on the verge of deployment, 3GPP is driving its implementation by defining a versatile core network architecture, referred to as the 5G System, which integrates both 4G and 5G access networks. To address the growing diversity of 5G use cases, 3GPP is also addressing the need for a self-configuring core network architecture to adapt to various 5G scenarios. To meet this need, the concept of self-organizing core networks has been introduced to minimize manual configuration and maintenance efforts. This paper delves into the fundamental principles behind developing a self-organizing core network architecture, specifically tailored to 5G systems, and outlines a comprehensive set of procedures to enable the self organization of the core network, thereby enabling a automated and efficient management of the core network in 5G deployments. These procedures are designed to enable the core network to automatically configure itself, adapt to changing conditions, and maintain itself with minimal manual intervention.

Acoustic units of speech can be utilized to create speech models without requiring any initial knowledge about the language, allowing for the synthesis of realistic human-like speech. By analyzing large amounts of untranscribed speech data from multiple languages, the Acoustic Speech Units model was developed. By clustering speech data without relying on any existing knowledge of the language, the model captures the underlying characteristics of the speech signal. The AsuTTS system then uses a sequence-to-sequence model to convert written text into a sequence of these acoustic units, which can be played back to create a complete speech signal. The accuracy of the synthesized speech was evaluated using the naturalness of the speech signal and the movement of a robotic face that was controlled by the acoustic units. The results showed that the speech produced using Acoustic Speech Units sounded just as natural as a speech that was recorded without any editing.

Achieving optimal results in quadratic programming (QP) is a challenging task, 
especially when dealing with non-convex problems, which often results in local 
minima that can trap optimization algorithms. To address this issue, we take advantage 
of problem structure by breaking it down into a multi-stage problem and applying 
data-driven linear approximations of non-convex constraints using "McCormick 
envelopes." This approach allows us to exploit the relationship between variables 
and their impacts on cost functions and constraints to create effective linear 
relaxations. These costly linear approximations are then used asQP constraints within 
a motion planning framework. This method enables us to take advantage of efficient 
QP solvers and local trajectory refinement to achieve a balance between 
computational speed and optimality.

One key concept in quantum information is the ability to convert one state to another using stochastic methods, with information theory setting the limit on these transformations. However, previously proposed methods to identify states that can't be transformed have relied heavily on specific assumptions, such as maintaining the states' rank. Our research provides a universal criterion for determining the stochastic transformability of any quantum states, without being limited to particular methods. Our method identifies pairs of states between which stochastic transformation is impossible, revealing that the well-known Heisenberg limit isn't the only barrier and a similar protocol allows for processing a quadratic number of items without accessing each individually. Moreover, our research shows that probabilistic convolution of two uniform superpositions is inherently impossible, providing a rigorous proof of a previously open question.

The movement of a liquid within a cup resembles a swinging pendulum, but the liquid's properties make the analogy imperfect. The goal of this research paper is to develop a model that accurately describes the liquid's movement. This model will consider the liquid as particles interacting with each other and the container walls. A comparison with the behavior of grains in the same situation will also be conducted. Ultimately, the findings of this study have implications for understanding the behavior of liquid in moving containers, such as airplanes.

In the field of machine learning, a significant challenge arises when training algorithms are susceptible to perturbations that can disrupt their performance. This issue is particularly acute in scenarios where data is distributed unevenly across multiple nodes in a network, each node having its own local dataset. Recent research has addressed this problem by incorporating robust statistics into centralized algorithms, but such methods are not easily adaptable to decentralized settings. In response, a new approach, a two-time scale stochastic algorithm, is introduced in this study to address the challenge. This algorithm allows for the calculation of the robust mean without requiring an exhaustive search, by approximating it through consecutive updates of a dual variable. When applied to decentralized training, the algorithm results in a well-defined optimization problem, characterized by a trade-off between model accuracy and risk. Under specific conditions, the algorithm's convergence rate is analyzed and confirmed.

We examine the creation of initial energy and particle formation in ultra-relativistic nuclear collisions using a pre-equilibrium model based on the kinetic theory of the Boltzmann equation. This approach generates an initial energy profile and thermalizes over time, aligning with hydrodynamic expectations. Different particle generation methods produce varying final flow patterns. However, regardless of initial energy or particle creation approach, an universal behavior emerges after equilibrium is reached, indicating that hydrodynamic dynamics are independent of pre-equilibrium dynamics once thermalization occurs.

Research on line-interaction mapping reveals that the velocity distribution of molecular outflows from young stellar objects is not uniform, characterized by multiple distinct velocity components rather than a single Gaussian profile. This outcome contradicts the widely held theory that high-velocity jets from young stellar objects originate directly from accretion processes. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose an alternative explanation in which the observed molecular outflows are not purely the direct result of accretion, but instead consist of the direct emission from the surrounding envelope and the ionized emission from the ionized nebula. This model effectively accounts for the observed velocity distribution of molecular outflows. Furthermore, this theory is supported by the finding that the ionized components in molecular outflows tend to have lower velocities compared to their neutral counterparts. This is attributed to the fact that ionized gas is more confined to the immediate vicinity of the protostar due to radiation pressure, whereas neutral gas can be pushed further away by pressure from the ionized component. This phenomenon is evident in the observed velocity distribution of the SO(1-0) P(2) and [S II] $\lambda$6717, [S II] $\lambda$6731 lines.

This study develops an equilibrated control method that simultaneously enhances performance and robustness in nonlinear systems subject to limitations. The proposed method adjusts the performance of predefined nonlinear controllers, including backstepping, high-gain observers, and robust control, by modifying their parameters. A key aspect of this approach involves optimizing a specific equilibration metric that balances desired performance and constraint satisfaction. This technique is demonstrated with two nonlinear examples, showing its effectiveness in achieving predefined performance levels and ensuring stability within system constraints.

Recent developments in space solar power systems have led to a growing interest in utilizing solar sails for space propulsion. However, maintaining the position and orientation of these spaceships can be challenging, particularly when maintaining a specific resonance is involved. Maintaining certain aspects of the orbit may also result in unwanted changes to other orbital parameters. To maintain the desired resonance, constant adjustments to the spacecraft's orbit are necessary, which in turn require precise knowledge of the system's dynamics. Despite these complexities, existing models for predicting the effects of solar radiation on spacecraft orbits are often too inaccurate or overly complicated, limiting their practical use. To address this issue, this study presents a new analytical approach to calculating the long-term resonant behavior of orbits affected by solar radiation pressure. This model is validated against numerical simulations and shows promising results in matching the accuracy of more advanced numerical methods. By comparing the time evolution of key orbital parameters, it is demonstrated that the new analytical model provides a satisfactory approximation of the more complex numerical solution.

Advanced materials science, particularly those involving typical semiconductors, can be effectively studied using the tight-binding model. However, a fundamental issue arises when attempting to perform periodic boundary conditions on a single atom. Since no atom can fit perfectly into an infinite lattice without creating an inconsistency, a 'missing atom' scenario emerges. To address this problem, we propose a new solution. By applying a specific map to the Hamiltonian, we show that the 'missing atom' scenario is effectively a free-electron gas. To maintain the integrity of the electron system, an additional term representing a specific potential is applied. Our findings indicate that applying this potential results in a potential of approximately 0.07 Rydbergs. Our model has been validated for silicon and shows that the 'vacancy' contribution can be neglected when this potential is applied. Our work provides a practical approach for calculating and converging the properties of common semiconductors using the t*Basis code.

This research introduces a system that utilizes semantic keypoints to determine the identity, 3D position, and shape of objects in various settings. Building on existing methods that combine visual and category-specific information to identify unique keypoints, our approach extends this concept to also deduce the location and shape of entire objects. We establish connections between keypoint trajectories and overall object structure by creating abstract paths and leveraging category-specific prior knowledge. We propose a novel optimization framework that incorporates these elements and allows for the application of uncertainty theory to enhance robustness against disruptions at the keypoints level. Additionally, our method can adapt to objects with altered structures by incorporating prior knowledge about 3D shapes and adjusting the optimization process accordingly. This approach is demonstrated on datasets representing airplanes and humans.

This study introduces a novel approach for determining the intervals of estimation for parameters from datasets following a Cauchy distribution. The method employed leverages the concept of posterior distributions. The analysis specifically focuses on deriving the interval for the location parameter using Bayes theorem, and explores two distinct scenarios based on different prior choices: one with Cauchy distribution, and another with a uniform distribution. Furthermore, the research provides the interval for the sample mean and evaluates the effectiveness of this estimation method through simulations.

A new design, known as the basket trial, is emerging as a popular approach for testing multiple related hypotheses with distinct patient populations. To utilize efficiency and statistical borrowing among related patient populations, we develop a Bayesian method to determine optimal sample sizes. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach yields accurate predictions and can prevent both under-sampling and over-sampling. Notably, we find that the predicted sample sizes often exceed those obtained in previous pre-posterior assessments.

This study proposes a revised sequential loop tightening strategy to enhance linear quadratic (LQ) optimal control for motion systems with varying characteristics. By accounting for system constraints and uncertainties, each sub-system is designed to ensure closed-loop stability and satisfy specific performance criteria. A multi-dimensional Bode plot is utilized to assess stability margins in systems with varying parameters, forming the basis of sequential loop tightening. A successive LQ design process is then carried out for the decoupled single-input single-output systems. The proposed method is demonstrated to effectively handle constraints and robustness requirements in complex motion systems, as seen in the development of a high-precision telescope's stabilization system with an optically compensated tilt sensor.

Deep learning has become a highly effective tool for generating high-quality synthetic images, yet current rendering-based approaches are heavily dependent on complete 3D models and extensive point clouds. In contrast, there are increasing applications for 2.5D 3D visual models in areas such as augmented reality and robotics, but these models lack the capability to handle large-scale alignment tasks due to their relatively small overlap. Our research introduces PRNet, a novel approach that uses projection and rasterization to learn the alignment of partial point clouds through a self-supervised framework. By integrating both local and global geometric self-supervision, PRNet can accurately align disparate point clouds, outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods in challenging scenarios. Furthermore, our method has demonstrated the ability to learn robust 2.5D projection operators, enabling the effective alignment of both 2.5D and 3D point cloud scenarios.

The $R_\infty$ property, which signifies an infinite number of isomorphism classes of groups with a specific structure, is being analyzed in relation to certain groups that build upon generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups through a series of central extensions. This structure allows us to associate each group with a particular nilpotent quotient, and it has been shown that this quotient possesses the $R_\infty$ property, which was first demonstrated by C. Maier and his colleagues.

Current measurements of the Standard Model's vacuum suggest it's metastable, with a potential true vacuum of lower energy.  A key question arises as to whether this false vacuum will eventually transition to the true vacuum through quantum tunneling, an event that would have profound implications for the universe.  To verify the existence of this true vacuum, we need to find the point of intersection between two lines in the space of Higgs and top quark masses.  This requires a precise determination of the top quark mass to within 1 MeV, as well as a 10 equivalent times improvement in the Higgs mass measurement.  We examine various potential collider combinations that can achieve these goals, with a primary focus on the future colliders such as the electron-positron Higgs factory and the electron-ion collider, in addition to the existing top quark factory.

In time-resolved spectroscopy, analyzing how molecules and materials change over time is crucial. This research aims to develop a reliable method for determining structural and electronic characteristics from time-sensitive absorption spectra. The approach uses artificial neural networks to create a dynamic framework that can calculate the optical properties of non-equilibrium molecular systems over a period of time. The network is trained based on the specific molecules or materials under study, allowing it to predict their evolving absorption spectra. The optimization process then generates a series of possible configurations over time, starting with an initial unknown state. These configurations are adjusted to minimize the difference between the calculated and experimentally measured absorption spectra. The calculations reveal that a key aspect of the approach is its resilience to noise, enabling accurate results even in the presence of significant measurement errors. Additionally, a notable feature is its capability to accurately model overlapping electronic transitions. This robustness has been demonstrated through the analysis of excited-state absorption spectra of benzene and a series of excited-state spectra obtained from two different iodine isotopes.

The study calculates and compares the distribution profiles of the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons, with some profiles analogous to particle mass distribution functions. Utilizing the Bethe-Salpeter amplitude for the vector and axial vector mesons, the profiles are determined through light-front wave functions, and the study also computes the spins associated with these mesons, which align with the standard quark model.

We on purpose avoid the use of Fourier transform to describe subspaces of Schwartz functions, specifically those that decay exponentially along with their derivatives, particularly on the non-commutative torus. Our method employs direct characterizations by decay rates, which enable us to demonstrate the effectiveness of Toeplitz operators between distinct Gelfand-Shilov spaces on the non-commutative torus.

Segmentation of uncommon imaging modalities is a challenging task due to the high annotation cost and scarcity of data. To overcome this, researchers have explored the potential of pre-trained models from other modalities. However, directly transferring labels from one modality to another often yields subpar results. To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel cyclic division generative adversarial network that leverages the power of iterative refinement to adapt pre-trained models. This approach allows for more accurate segmentation on the target modality, a goal we have successfully achieved by attaining a mean intersection over union of 0.7105 on the Retina dataset.

A significant hurdle in sequence-based action classification is overcoming the limitation of traditional RNNs which typically classify entire action sequences at once, resulting in lower accuracy. Our solution involves combining an RNN with the test-time adaptation technique and mapping actions onto an infinite RBF kernel Hilbert space. This approach enables each test sequence to be classified individually without training. Our extensive experiments on three datasets have demonstrated the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art techniques.

A comprehensive analysis of the massive UV flare from AD Leo in 1985 was conducted using a flare plasma model. This model effectively explained the observed data from the OSO-7 satellite. The analysis revealed a high flare plasma density of around 10^11 cm^-3. The plasma temperature increased from 2.5 MK to 3.5 MK over the course of the flare. The electron number in the plasma increased significantly, rising from 10^42 to 10^43. The X-ray emission from the flare peaked at a luminosity of 10^31 erg/s. The analysis also showed that the UV lines were caused by two distinct flare plasma components.

We are examining the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. A key connection we establish is between the linearized operator acting on the moment map image of the deformation theory and the twisted Dirac operator. From this relationship, we derive the Kervaire invariant as an obstruction to infiniitesimal deformations. Additionally, we identify an integration-by-parts formula that separates the deformation theory into two components: the cohomology represented by the twisting spinors and the standard first-order cohomology of the manifold. In the specific case of nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ deformations of the product of the round sphere and circle with itself, we demonstrate that the space of nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ deformations corresponds to the harmonic 3-forms.

This paper examines the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\phi$ and the weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \phi}$ are normal and $C$-normal when acting on the Hardy space $H^2$ of the unit disk.

Given a prime number p, we will refer to a sequence as a p-core p'-sequence if it's core is divisible by all prime numbers other than p. Our research focuses on the length of the longest p-core p'-sequences, where the core elements are all different and we will denote this maximum length as l(p). It turns out that this length can be broken down into the sum of a base value and a variable value related to a set of prime numbers. Specifically, this length equals the base value plus the sum of the logarithms of the elements in a set of prime numbers less than or equal to it, and the elements in this set are all different and different from p. This discovery leads to an algorithmic method to calculate l(p) for any given prime number p, and we will illustrate this method with examples of the calculated lengths for all prime numbers up to 100. Additionally, we will connect the problem of finding the longest p-core p'-sequences to the problem of finding the longest walks on a graph that represents addition in the residue field of p.

Our proposed method, Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), tackles the challenge in point cloud processing by converting a generic, unrefined mesh into a sleek surface that retains the original shape's characteristics under various transformations. We've developed two distinct approaches for TPC, one that seeks the shape's true intrinsic geometry and another aims to map the rough mesh to a clean surface within a predetermined distance. The problem's difficulty is reduced to its essential components, enabling state-of-the-art results in various smoothening tasks. Notably, our SUSTAIN model, built upon TPC, achieves exceptional smoothening results with minimal detail loss, outperforming existing techniques by marginally reducing error while maintaining or even improving shape consistency.

In a network of Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radars, multiple devices may transmit at the same time, leading to interference and limiting the distance at which targets can be detected. To address this issue, two methods inspired by wireless communication protocols, specifically slotted ALOHA and carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA), are being explored to allow multiple radars to coexist and operate at the same frequency. However, standard protocols are not suitable for FMCW radar systems due to the significant time delay involved in measuring distance. As a result, these protocols have been modified to meet the needs of FMCW radar networks, taking into account factors such as detection range and transmitted power. A comparison of the modified slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols is presented, along with a discussion on the potential for using these methods in a practical FMCW radar system, including a consideration of the additional processing required and the ability to distinguish between successful and contested transmissions.

This entry initiates a theoretical investigation into how Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is impacted by entangled two-photon absorption (E-TPA) processes, which occur when a photon pair interacts with a qubit, causing a transition from an excited state back to the ground state and emitting two photons. Notably, such interactions can take place even when the input photons are entangled. In the case where E-TTP affects photons that are not absorbed, they remain in a coherent state, leading to a modification in the output state. Consequently, absorptive interference patterns emerge, characterized by outcomes dependent on absorption parameters, although the anti-correlation of photon detections persists. In contrast, in situations where absorbed photons are not present, absorptive interference patterns arise, resulting in reduced correlations in photon outputs. In addition, our analysis explores how variations in system parameters, including detuning and anisotropic absorption, influence absorptive interference, as well as potential applications in photonic quantum information processing.

Temporal knowledge graph completion (KGC) is a critical task involving predicting missing entity relationships across multiple temporal contexts. Current research has a significant gap in addressing KGC under a sparse data scenario, where most available data points are absent in the graph. This paper bridges this gap by assuming that learned continuous representations of relations are space-compressible, thereby allowing models to generalize effectively to unseen facts. Building upon this premise, two novel theories are developed: compressing relations to a compact, low-dimensional space and aggregating multiple temporal embeddings of a single entity factor, both of which contribute to improved generalization. Our comprehensive empirical results confirm the significant benefits of these approaches, outperforming existing methods in the KGC field.

In the context of big bang cosmology, the rapid expansion phase known as the
"reheating" process is crucial. We've discovered through numerical simulations
that the influence of thermal noise from the surrounding plasma significantly
affects outcome variations. Our findings show that incorporating thermal noise
leads to more rapid and consistent particle generation compared to the deterministic
so-called "bounce" scenario previously proposed in literature. Furthermore, we've
observed the emergence of "locally adiabatic" outcomes, in which particle
production gradually diminishes. These discoveries have important implications for
understanding early universe evolution and could inform future research in this
area.

We have established a perfect correlation between shared randomness and the outcomes of specific binary measurements performed on quantum systems with two parties. This correlation demonstrates Bell nonlocality without the use of inequalities, even though the correlations do not allow for the unique identification of underlying nonlocal resources. Furthermore, both the nonlocal aspect and the absence of a local explanation of this correlation have been proven without recourse to inequalities. This outcome provides insight into novel aspects of Bell nonlocality and reveals new connections between nonlocal correlations and the tasks that can be accomplished through them.

We are revisiting the concept of flat lines in the context of Ricci-recurrent spaces with certain pre-defined constraints. Our analysis reveals new characterizations of flat lines that allow us to derive the general structure of 3-dimensional spaces with a specific type of Ricci curvature, as well as 5-dimensional spaces where a certain curvature operator exists. Additionally, we will examine the characteristics of space forms that can be conformally related to certain other 5-dimensional spaces.

Recent experimental studies have found that superconductivity in certain materials, such as hydrogen and carbon-based compounds, exhibits unusual characteristics with high transition temperatures and unusual behavior near the point where it becomes superconducting. Theoretical research has predicted that another material, YB hydride, possesses similar properties and their similarity to the previously studied superconducting compound MgB2 has led to the hypothesis that their high transition temperatures and unusual behavior may be caused by the presence of boron-based electronic states. The present research investigates the accuracy of this hypothesis by investigating the electronic and lattice properties of YB hydride, and the results show that the experimentally observed superconducting transition temperature of approximately 70K is not supported by the calculations. The predicted superconducting behavior in YB hydride is relatively weak and localized to the surface, with the experimental and theoretical results showing significant discrepancies. The predicted superconducting transition temperature of YB hydride is significantly lower than the experiment, and the predicted superconducting gap is also much smaller than the predicted gap in MgB2. The predicted superconducting gap is also much smaller than the predicted gap in MgB2. The predicted superconducting gap is also much smaller than the predicted gap in MgB2. The predicted superconducting gap is also much smaller than the predicted gap in MgB2.

In a cloud-based infrastructure, deciding how to allocate tasks to servers is crucial for optimal resource distribution and operational efficiency. This decision is complicated by the varying number of tasks and available servers, which often results in an unbalanced allocation across servers. This study examines the task server (TS) allocation problem under circumstances where the task counts on servers follow a specific mathematical pattern known as the flattened partition model. Our analysis focuses on two key scenarios - the known and unknown cases - and evaluates TS allocation strategies under the constraint of not exceeding each server's capacity. This research also considers the M/G/∞ queue model, which can approximate a wide range of run allocation scenarios, to derive allocation policies based on either a single or multiple servers' observations. These policies show significant improvements in task counts compared to random allocation, with gains increasing proportionally to the square of the observation batch size. Furthermore, we explore an alternative optimization approach that prioritizes maximizing the likelihood of achieving optimal resource utilization across servers.

In recent research, the second white dwarf mass limit is being studied as a possible indicator to solve the long-standing neutron star mass range issue. We investigate the low-temperature behavior of the partition function by applying a character-theoretic approach, which allows us to establish mass limits for the Galois representations associated with certain families of modular forms. This largely completes a previous study initiated by the author and T. character for the full group 2 in GL_2/Z. We demonstrate that the mass limits we derive from this approach are consistent with the masses determined by 2-volume arguments, and we observe that the mass limits are influenced by the stiffness of the arithmetic groups. By utilizing basic properties of sup-norm bounds and the spectrum of Hecke operators, we establish stiffness estimates for several subsets of the full group 2 in GL_2/Z, and we establish arithmetic mass limits. This investigation reveals that the mass limits are affected by the geometry of the locally symmetric space and its symmetry.

High-speed automation systems like those found in vehicles demand exceptional speed and reliability. When their primary system fails, backup support becomes crucial. Formally validating systems with fail-over capabilities is challenging due to their complex and potentially hazardous nature. In this research, a fail-operational automotive driving system was validated using formal methods, using a model based on Tidal, a programming language suitable for safety-crealations. The team employed Relational Hoare Logic to establish the model's correctness and then submitted it to the KeY tool for automatic verification.

This research proposes an advanced algorithm for categorizing complex systems in response to external stimuli. The proposed method involves a two-step process: first, identifying distinct states in the system that result from varying levels of influence, and second, organizing these states based on their differences. The algorithm's ability to extract relevant information from complex systems has been demonstrated using a range of examples, including the impact of external forces on a simple system, wind effects on different types of birds, and the influence of external forces on systems with and without certain characteristics.

Infinitesimal calculus has been the most influential mathematical development of the last four centuries, yet it remains challenging to explain the underlying concepts in a way that is both intuitive and mathematically rigorous. Historically, Leibnizian calculus relied on informal arguments that were later dismissed due to logical inconsistencies. This account explores three modern mathematical frameworks - non-standard analysis, smoothness of functions, and axiomatic approach to infinitesimals - that have been established in the 20th and 21st centuries to give a solid foundation to Leibnizian calculus. These frameworks provide rigorous foundations for key concepts such as infinitesimal and infinitely large numbers, as well as the derivatives and differentials that were central to Leibnizian calculus.

We've developed a model for radio intensity mapping that accounts for how hydrogen in the universe affects signal measurements, particularly for early HI. This model considers the fluctuations in HI due to the large-scale structure of the universe, as well as the background radiation and stationary noise from the universe itself. By comparing the model's predictions with real data, researchers can better understand how the universe's noise is affected and can better remove the noise from the signal. The model also helps in determining the best strategies for optimizing experiments and can help in assessing the impact of foreground removal on the signal. For instance, the model shows that common foreground removal methods, such as polynomial fitting and principal component analysis, can introduce artifacts in the signal that need to be taken into account.

Independent sets within countable graphs serve as a model for understanding and developing efficient protocols to identify and count these sets in real-time. We've achieved this goal by creating a family of independent sets in specific types of grids, where each new set's size exceeds the previous one by an infinitely extendable margin. To accomplish this, we've created a set of finite-state machines that can update their settings based on input.

In recent years, recommender systems have experienced significant growth and development. Various types of systems have been designed, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. Despite this, researchers continue to explore innovative approaches to improve their capabilities. This paper explores a novel method that combines two prominent techniques, namely context-aware and behavior-based recommender systems, to enhance their individual performance. A thorough examination of existing techniques, along with a detailed analysis of a proposed hybrid system, will be presented.

We demonstrate that a specific polynomial modification of random matrix expressions is a continuous transformation, a significant result essential to our approach. Leveraging this finding, we resolve the long-standing openness issue for certain matrix ensembles, including Gaussian Beta ensembles and their real and complex counterparts. Additionally, we prove that sample vectors drawn from these ensembles exhibit a specific property known as type $B$ conditional freeness, a relationship we establish within the context of a common probability space.

This study proposes a novel, intuitive method to verify properties of complex, concurrent systems over infinite sequences of observations, specifically in the context of real-time aspects, by integrating elements of metric temporal logic and logic on ordered structures. It's then demonstrated that this method is equally expressive as the latter. The investigation is further extended to consider two-metric temporal reasoning, which continues to be as expressive as the original framework. Ultimately, the study is contextualized within the broader field of model checking, and its implications are discussed in relation to existing research.

The experimentally observed $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ blending in $\eta \pi^+$ from
$e^+e^- \to \pi^+ \pi^- a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ resonances is investigated in
$\psi'(3S) \to a_0(980)-f_0(980) \gamma$ vector meson dominance model.  Our study
reveals that the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ mass degeneracy and the vector
$a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ vector meson dominance hold true, but the mass shift of these
resonances is not applicable in this context.  Notably, the $a_0(980)$ line shape
exhibits isospin breaking without mass shift, in contrast to theories
predicting a mass shift.  Consequently, a new line shape model is introduced and
utilized to investigate the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ interference in $\bar B_s^0
\to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ decays.  Simulation results from a new Monte Carlo are
provided and a minimum $a_0(980)$ fraction of 1

The GRAVITY ruling camera is a groundbreaking invention that combines four high-performance 2D scientific CMOS sensors to generate a customizable, reconfigurable image with a vast 1.7 arcmin x 1.7 arcmin field of view and variable fields of view ranging from 0.25 arcsec to 1 arcsec. Developed in collaboration with the Max-Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics and ESO, this innovative device has been extensively characterized, and the resulting performance metrics have demonstrated its exceptional quality. The ruling camera's fields of view, efficiency, resolution, and stability have all been carefully analyzed, and the results have confirmed its capacity to track and capture the movement of various celestial objects within a 1.7 arcmin x 1.7 arcmin field of view with sub-arcsec precision. Furthermore, the ruling camera's real-time processing capabilities have been put to the test, and the results have shown its ability to process data at a rate of 100 Mbps and reconstruct images within a fraction of a second.

The objective of the k-Generalized k-Center problem is to select k subsets within a given instance of the k-Generalized k-Clique problem, such that the maximum distance between any two selected subsets is minimized. We demonstrate that, under the assumption that P is not equal to NP, there is no constant-factor approximation algorithm feasible on a constant doubling graph, whereas a constant-factor approximation is possible for a constant freeway graph, even if the number of subsets, k, is exponentially large. This result provides a unique instance where the efficiency of NP-hard approximation algorithms is significantly impacted by a subtle geometric property, with the two graphs being locally isometric yet possessing vastly different approximation capabilities.
This paper aims to prove uniqueness theoreles for entire functions based on their partial arguments, with related results also provided.

This research paper explores an early exit strategy for solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations using a Gröbner basis approach, incorporating errors. We have refined some evaluation criteria and achieved faster computation times.

The dynamic behavior of an ensemble of interacting two-state atoms, protected by parity symmetry, was analyzed. The presence of radiative interactions, a hallmark of electromagnetic theory, was incorporated into the examination. The system's energy eigenstates exhibited either even or odd parity, each associated with a distinct lifetime. The eigenstates' parity was found to dictate the way in which it could decay. The eigenstates' properties were found to depend on the fine-structure constant. Moreover, a protection of certain eigenstates from decaying, unique to this system, was identified. The uniqueness of this feature sets it apart from other electromagnetic system features. The properties of certain eigenstates, such as their separation and decay rates, exhibited parabolic patterns as the interatomic distance increased. In addition, as the number of atoms in the ensemble increased, certain eigenstates exhibited altered properties, such as changed separation and decay rates. The separation of certain eigenstates showed an exponential decrease with increasing interatomic distance. The decay rates of certain eigenstates showed altered behavior, such as a change in sign, in certain regions. The parity of certain eigenstates influenced their emission properties. The eigenstates' properties were found to exhibit symmetry under the transformation of certain parameters. The system's eigenstates exhibited package emission, where multiple photons are emitted simultaneously. The package emission probability showed an exponential decrease as the number of atoms in the ensemble increased. The system's eigenstates exhibited symmetry under the transformation of certain parameters.

We have developed a straightforward yet highly accurate analytical model for the equilibrium thermodynamic properties of an alkali plasma. Our research utilizes the path integral formalism to calculate the interaction energy of the nucleus and the surrounding electrons. By combining this calculation with the ideal gas model for the core of the atom's valence electron, we obtained precise estimates for key thermodynamic properties. These estimates are then compared with computer simulations, specifically Monte Carlo methods, demonstrating excellent agreement. Furthermore, our theoretical results show significant agreement with existing model potential calculations for a specific plasma consisting of potassium ions.

This study explores the behavior of vector mesons, specifically $\rho$ and $w$, in a environment characterized by chiral asymmetry, characterized by the difference between the numbers of left and right-handed fermions. The research is grounded in the local potential approximation of the real-time Green function, with the primary focus on understanding the spectrum of these mesons in the presence of a background of chiral fermions, resulting from the polarization of these fermions. The analysis reveals that the masses of the $\rho$ and $w$ mesons exhibit distinct responses: the mass of the $\rho$ meson remains unchanged, whereas the mass of the $w$ meson acquires a non-zero value. The research also identifies the conditions necessary for the spectrum of vector mesons to remain real.

This research focuses on developing an algorithm to estimate the scale of a network when assuming a specific underlying structure, which is based on a two-tier framework of hub and peripheral nodes. We are particularly interested in scenarios where legitimate nodes communicate with each other to gauge network size. To begin, we created a consensus algorithm that relies on a trusted node to determine the network scale under assumption A. Subsequently, we developed a more robust algorithm, without a designated authority, capable of producing accurate estimations under assumption B, even in the presence of Byzantine faulty nodes. Furthermore, we explored and tested the performance of our algorithm in a real-world setting, utilizing a platform called NetSim.

This research introduces a new computational strategy to create numerical initial data sets for general relativity simulations. The method involves modifying the standard conformal-transverse-traceless decomposition by first establishing the extrinsic curvature's traceless component before determining its trace. By decoupling the Hamiltonian constraint from this conformal transformation, we allow the initial data to be more freely chosen. Specifically, the lapse function and a part of the extrinsic curvature's trace can now be independently selected. A systematic approach is provided for converting any initial data set into a set satisfying the Hamiltonian constraint through conformal scaling. Additionally, the method's performance is evaluated in two key areas: its ability to generate compact binary black hole data and the data required for simulating shock waves in relativistic jets.

Our research involves creating and testing mass-produced, large-diameter PMTs, specifically 20-inch models, which are crucial for the Jiangmen Underwater Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) project. We have created these PMTs in batches using a carefully controlled production process. To assess their performance, we conducted thorough testing and analysis using automated systems. The results show that our PMTs have excellent and consistent characteristics in terms of linearity, gain stability, and temporal resolution. Additionally, the effect of operating at high voltage on the PMTs' performance in various environments, including different temperatures and pressures, has been thoroughly investigated.

Recent research on multivariate time series forecasting using neural networks has achieved impressive results. Nonetheless, existing methods typically employ a fixed network structure, which may not be optimal. This paper proposes an innovative approach called Multidimensional Time Series Analysis with Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks (MTSAGA). By representing the given time series data as a dynamic graph, MTSAGA automatically generates a network structure that is tailored to the input. This novel method enables graph convolutional networks to capture both the local and global dependencies within the time series data. Moreover, MTSAGA is universal and can be applied to any multivariate time series forecasting tasks. Experimental findings demonstrate that models based on MTSAGA consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines on nine benchmark datasets across four distinct domains, showcasing MTSAGA's efficacy in enhancing time series forecasting.

Astronomers use a device called an atmospheric dispersion corrector (ADC) to correct for the differential dispersion that occurs in telescopes.  Researchers have developed multiple models to describe how ADCs work, but these models were previously only based on lab experiments.  We've obtained real-world data from the ADC on the ESO Paranal 2.6-m telescope and compared it to three different models: one for a simple prism, another for a Blaser, and a model that accounts for the use of mirrors.  We found that the measured data can accurately predict ADC performance down to angles as small as 10 arcseconds.  We observed that the real-world data doesn't match either the Blaser or the prism model alone, suggesting that a combination of both is likely responsible.  We've also discovered that dust on the Blaser's mirrors could explain the observed discrepancies, and we've worked out how to use this information to correct for the effect of dust on the ADC's performance.

In the realm of deep learning, labeled distillation enables models to leverage a few golden data points for significant performance enhancements. Most current approaches rely on a small number of expert instructors, but this limits their effectiveness as it necessitates multiple instructors for a noticeable improvement. To address this problem, we introduce a novel framework, denoted as Pairwise Iterative Learner for Ensemble (PILE), which employs an ensemble of pairwise comparisons to create a self-improving labeling process. By utilizing only a single instructor, our method dynamically generates labels for unlabeled data, thereby avoiding the bottleneck associated with limited expert input. Empirical results show that PILE achieves comparable outcomes to a full ensemble of instructors, even with as few as two data points from a single expert.

We suggest detecting ultralight bosonic shadow matter through a correlation function analysis of detector data, which would be less susceptible to noise than other detection methods. Our approach involves a 'bifurcated detector array configuration,' in which nearby detector arrays experience distinct gravitational wave field fluctuations. This configuration enables a detector separation far exceeding the de Broglie wavelength of the particle cloud. Our simulation results indicate that detector outputs show a measurable signal when exposed to ultralight bosonic shadow matter.

A discrete version of basis pursuit is a well-known method for solving underdetermined linear systems by finding the sparsest solution with minimum l1-norm.  The problem can be formulated as an optimization task involving a convex function subject to a set of linear constraints.  Due to the presence of kinks in the objective function, standard duality theory is not directly applicable.  To address this, a concept of weak duality has been introduced and used to establish a novel connection between the uniqueness of solutions in basis pursuit and specific geometric properties.  This relationship allows for the formulation of a novel, verifiable condition for sparse solution uniqueness.  The approach can also be extended to a continuous variant of the problem, providing insights into the underlying duality.

P4 has become a widely adopted language for configuring network devices, with support from major switch vendors including Intel and Broadcom. These devices have unique architectures that require separate compiler backends. Our work fills a gap by creating an open-source compiler backend compatible with both types of devices, aiming for the Data Plane Development Environment environment. We evaluated our compiler using real traffic and achieved significant performance improvements, with up to a 4x increase in utilization compared to the existing P416 compiler backend.

In numerical methods using the finite element approach, the vector transport equation can be efficiently resolved by employing the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements. However, approximating this equation by directly discretizing the continuous problem results in poor first-order convergence rates. To rectify this issue, we rephrase the problem using a mixed finite element formulation. By applying a novel multigrid method that utilizes the least-squares problems from both coarse and fine levels, we successfully achieve a robust solver that maintains an algorithmic complexity of O( log(n) * m), where 'm' represents the total number of unknowns. Moreover, we show that a local problem can be easily and efficiently resolved by exploiting the structure of the matrix, rendering it diagonal, which enables an O(1) solution time. To streamline our multigrid solver and ensure robustness, we introduce a new technique to tackle the local problems, involving the exploitation of a problem's local structure to derive a suitable approximation.

Distributed machine learning is a well-established concept, with multiple strategies available to resolve a specific optimization issue across various network topologies. A significant challenge arises when considering bias in automated decision-making systems, a concern amplified by high-profile cases. Emerging as a promising solution, Federated Learning (FL) leverages a central server and multiple client devices to inherently implement train-and-share approach. This approach offers both computational and privacy advantages, given that participation in FL-based training does not require sharing sensitive user data. Our study delves into how FL impacts two primary methods - shared model training and distributed robust encodings. We also assess the impact of FL on two key aspects: fairness and privacy. Our research indicates that FL's influence on encodings may exacerbate biases, whereas the use of FL with a model may improve encodings' fairness. Furthermore, FL contributes to a model's privacy by utilizing smaller batch sizes and reducing user information exposure.

Using 13.6 inverse femtobarns of $\pp$ collision data, collected at the LHCb experiment, we have conducted a sensitive search for the presence of a particular excited state, known as $3^3\Sigma_\rho$, in the decay of a specific particle, the $B_c^+$, into a $J/\psi$ and a pion. This search was performed for particles with a specific invariant mass range and was carried out over three distinct resonance peaks. As a result, we have observed one state, which matches theoretical predictions, while the other two states were not observed and limits on their formation have been set.

This research introduces a family of one-parameter estimates, continuous-stage Runge-Kutta formulas, for the standard numerical resolution of the ordinary differential equation $y'(t) = f(t, y(t))$, with a given initial condition $y(0) = y_0$, where $t_y$ denotes a target time to be determined. The value of $t_y$ is an element of the set of non-negative real numbers. The proposed solutions build upon the principles outlined in the paper "On the approximation of some differential equations".

Recent breakthroughs in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have revolutionized many tasks, but their substantial computational requirements pose a significant obstacle to their widespread adoption, especially for models like the Transformer that demand even greater processing power. Utilizing GPUs in combination can mitigate this limitation, although current methods have several drawbacks, such as reduced training speed and the risk of data duplication. This study introduces an innovative approach called Regional Critic Training (RCT), which enables DNN learning to scale across multiple GPUs without splitting the model or data, thereby optimizing resource utilization and preserving data diversity. By employing this method, researchers have successfully accelerated the training of DNNs on various datasets, including ImageNet, and achieved comparable results to other techniques, such as data parallel learning, while outperforming them in terms of speed.

Despite their theoretical significance, three-dimensional chaotic systems exhibiting non-attracting, fractal invariant sets have received less attention compared to their two-dimensional counterparts. We investigate how a three-dimensional repeller responds to weak dissipation in a scattering setup using a scaled model of the H\'enon-Heiles system. Our findings reveal that non-linear stretching of the repeller significantly differs from its two-dimensional equivalent. Furthermore, we observe that weak dissipation leads to the ejection of three-dimensional islands and enhances the measure of three-dimensional Wada basins.
