successfully replicate the full range of counting abilities exhibited by children.
This study introduces a neural network model that not only mimics the progression
of basic counting concepts but also demonstrates the ability to learn patterns
beyond its training data, akin to human-like intelligence. By providing insights
into effective training methods for tasks that are challenging for machines to
master, this research has far-reaching implications for using AI to understand
and simulate higher cognitive processes.

Bloom filters are widely used probabilistic data structures, but they consume excessive memory, causing multiple items to be represented by the same bit. This issue is mitigated by iterative bit manipulation, yet such methods are computationally intensive. A similar problem arises with cuckoo filters, which also suffer from considerable memory consumption. To address this problem, a new probabilistic data structure called the xor filter has been proposed, which is capable of faster insertion and query operations, while minimizing memory usage and eliminating the need for expensive CPU instructions.
This letter's purpose is to establish connections between two mathematical fields - convex analysis and convex geometry - based on analogous concepts and constructions within each domain.

In this research, we aim to establish a theoretical framework that can quantify the influence of future price changes on current price trends. By incorporating future price changes as relevant information, we can explain past and present price changes. Our proposed framework is based on a change in the market's probability distribution of future price changes, which can be captured by the Kullback-Leibler distance. This distance can explain current price trends and, combined with price changes, can determine the direction of those price changes. Additionally, we will define two new time series that can serve as leading and lagging indicators to price changes, which can be used to create a more robust index that can predict future price changes.

By combining the principles of differential privacy and secure lattice cryptography, a framework has been developed to address the limitations of federated learning, as well as its vulnerabilities to data manipulation and model inversion attacks. This innovation aims to create a reliable and secure federated learning environment, particularly for mobile devices with processing capabilities. A new framework, FLVoogd, integrates a private key server, creating a two-layer architecture for vertical and horizontal federated learning setups. This approach enables a trustworthy and secure communication channel, allowing participants to learn and update models without exposing sensitive data. Furthermore, a framework for federated object detection, FLVoogd-D, has been proposed, and its performance is evaluated on the COCO dataset.

Simulated environments are commonly used for developing and refining AI models, particularly in end-to-end autonomous driving applications. Nevertheless, a significant discrepancy exists between artificial and real-world data characteristics. This gap is exacerbated by differences in rendering methods and agent interactions. In an attempt to bridge this divide, transfer learning has been employed, but it has its limitations. Our research focuses on enhancing the transferability of simulated data to real-world data by leveraging the VAE framework. This approach involves training VAEs on both synthetic and real images, then using the encoding module to manipulate latent representations and the reconstruction network to improve the quality of artificial data, ultimately simulating a more realistic image distribution. Our proposed method is demonstrated on the task of end-to-end autonomous vehicle control.

In the age of information, false deepfakes have become a pressing concern, potentially leading to misinformation and harm. To address this, we are working on creating DeepfakeCounter, a framework designed to counteract malicious deepfakes by minimizing the effects of input variations and aligning detection methods for different types of input. Our framework begins with a comparison of deepfake detection methods, a task that has been largely overlooked in current research. Our analysis of existing approaches and the underlying data features has guided our design of a false deepfake generation module and corresponding detector. Our experimental results have shown that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in multiple scenarios, including changes in audio, scripts, faces, backgrounds, and the presence of masks.

Identifying the composition of sub-Neptune exoplanets is a major challenge in modern astronomy. Theoretical models suggest that many of these exoplanets could have solid surfaces with global oceans, though direct observation of such surfaces is hindered by cloudy atmospheres. By developing a new analytical approach, we have created a mathematical relationship that links atmospheric pressure and temperature to gas chemistry and ion balance. This relationship allows us to identify the surface temperature of exoplanets with minimal data. We applied this approach to two exoplanets, K2-3b and K2-3c, and found that their temperatures are consistent with a water world hypothesis. The proposed method provides a new tool for studying the composition of exoplanets, potentially providing the first direct evidence of global oceans on these planets.

Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing have been driven by the application of non-recurrent deep neural networks, yet the design of neuro-symbolic architectures that combine the benefits of recurrent and non-recurrent models remains an open challenge in neuroscience-inspired computing. This paper delves into the limitations of existing recurrent spiking neural networks when tasked with learning basic sequence models, such as the 9-tauri model, and demonstrates that these models are incapable of acquiring even this simple task without significant modifications. To address these shortcomings, we propose a revised architecture incorporating a k-winners-take-all mechanism and a multi-scale membrane potential system, which, in contrast to earlier designs, exhibit a feasible learning capability. Our enhanced model is further shown to align with experimental data from macaque prefrontal cortex studies, highlighting a crucial gap between the performance of spiking neural networks and the biological plausibility of their learning abilities.

This challenge report outlines the approach taken by teams participating in the
out-of-category track of the competition. The track's objective is to assess a model's
adaptability to unfamiliar data categories. Given the scarcity of existing solutions,
our challenge report serves as a comprehensive guide, detailing the challenges and
potential strategies for designing a method that can handle novel categories of
data. The evaluation process involves two stages: during the pre-training phase, a model
is exposed to a diverse set of visual concepts, and in the adaptation phase, a model
trained on 20% of pre-training data from a new category is evaluated on the
remaining 80%. Performance is measured based on how a model adapits to categories
it wasn't pre-trained on.

A new approach to verifying Generalized Polynomial Chaos expansions is introduced, which is based on a novel variation of the Galerkin residual method specifically tailored for Component-Based representation formats. The primary goal of this approach is to provide reassurance that certain key characteristics of a low-dimensional approximated solution are accurately captured. This new method is more computationally efficient compared to traditional methods due to its reliance on compact data structures. The developed framework is demonstrated through two numerical examples, each providing reassurance at varying levels of computational expense relative to traditional methods.

This research focuses on developing an adaptive algorithm capable of detecting and isolating changes that occur in a Markov decision process (MDP) under partial observability. Building upon an established algorithm designed for fully observable sequential changes, the authors extend its principles to partially observable scenarios using particle filtering. Specifically, they devise a method to identify and pinpoint both incremental and catastrophic shifts in MDPs with parametric models. A theoretical analysis demonstrates the algorithm's ability to eventually detect any change and accurately isolate the type of shift within a finite number of steps. Furthermore, through numerical experiments, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in handling real-world applications.

This study focuses on the properties of two dwarf galaxies, NGC 1569 and IC 1613, through the analysis of their spectra. By examining their spectra, researchers have uncovered evidence of multiple starbursts in NGC 1569 that occurred at different times, specifically around 100 million years ago, 600 million years ago, and 1 billion years ago, as well as starbursts in IC 1613 that occurred around 1.3 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago, and 6 billion years ago. The research also found that the metal content of the two galaxies varied over time, with the metal content of NGC 1569 increasing rapidly in the early starbursts and then leveling off, while the metal content of IC 1613 increased gradually over time, following a power law. The research found that the metal content of the two galaxies was similar, with a power-law index of 2.2, and that the metal content of the two galaxies was affected by the initial abundance of deuterium and helium in the early universe.

We define and investigate a concept of homotopy action spectrum function-valued for profinite groups, with an established fixed point theory corresponding to continuous actions on compact ANRs. Additionally, we derive a formula for the equivariant cohomology of the product of two homotopy action spectra in terms of the fusion system associated with a p-subgroup of this group.

A key challenge in building advanced NLP models for documents is the high expense associated with data labeling required to achieve high performance. This problem is particularly pronounced for visually intricate document layouts. Our research focuses on significantly lowering the expense of data labeling by separating the tasks of formally structuring document content and recognizing individual sections, from the main goal of extracting specific data. This innovation allows us to leverage relatively cheap, non-expert labels to produce a set of sophisticated content structures and visual segmentations that can be automatically applied to new documents. This technique is then combined with data augmentation to enhance existing models and minimize the need for additional, expensive labeling. Our approach yields substantial cost reductions in fully trained models that outperform previous state-of-the-art systems in multiple document extraction tasks, while also providing pre-computed visual segmentations for immediate use in new document processing.

The EuS/InAs interface has garnered significant interest due to its potential for observing the magnetoelectric Kerr effect and its application as a topological insulator. To understand the influence of the interface on InAs's electronic properties, density functional theory was employed to investigate EuS/InAs heterostructures with different interfaces. Our research reveals that in a specific interface configuration, the topological surface states present in InAs's clean surface are eliminated, and the conduction and valence bands shift upward and downward respectively, within the InAs band gap, due to charge transfer from EuS. The interface also induces a localized magnetic moment at InAs's interface atoms, which could be relevant for exploring the magnetoelectric Kerr effect. Additionally, our findings show that the interface affects InAs's band structure, leading to a potential for engineering topological magnetic semiconductors through heterostructuring with InAs.

The relationship between Borel wadge classes can be described as a linear order, and we establish an effective method for determining if one class precedes another in this sequence. Specifically, given two continuous functions with target set emptiness confirmed, we prove their corresponding wadge classes' precedence relation by examining the functions themselves. This contributes to ongoing research effectively categorizing Borel sets linearly. As consequences, we obtain precise classifications for binary relations and a precise linear ordering of strong effective base classes.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown great potential in a range of applications, but their high computational and memory requirements often limit them to devices with significant processing power. While previous attempts to address this issue have focused on reducing the computational load by pruning the networks, they failed to address the memory constraint. This research introduces ClickTrain, a novel approach that precisely predicts the most critical operations in a DNN layer, allowing for the creation of extremely compact and efficient networks that can run on resource-constrained devices without compromising performance or training time. ClickTrain achieves this by introducing architectural preservation, fine-grained pruning, and a new evaluation metric, leading to reductions in model size and memory usage of up to 82% and 70%, respectively, while maintaining 90%+ of the accuracy of the original network.

This research examines how modal operators in non-classical linguistics influence the computation of Lambek Calculus by increasing complexity in proof verification but keeping it manageable in terms of co-complexity. It specifically looks at the distribution property of these modal operators and its impact on computational efficiency. Finding a co-complexity optimal proof system, the study uses automata theory to establish an upper limit on proof length within PTIME.

In the future of gravitational wave astronomy, the detection of neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) mergers will be made possible. These events possess unique characteristics in terms of gravitational wave signatures, differing from those of binary neutron star or binary black hole mergers. As a result, accurately identifying and categorizing NS-BH mergers is crucial. This work proposes a deep learning approach for classifying gravitational waves from NS-BH mergers. We utilized the GW190814 event, the first of its kind, and developed a convolutional neural network to classify a broad range of masses for more practical applications. The results indicate that our model achieved an accuracy of 99.9% on training data and 98.1% on testing data.

A comprehensive study of TOI-5542, a newly discovered exoplanetary system, is presented in this paper. Utilizing a combination of data from the TESS mission's second and third observing sectors, along with observations from the MEarth South project, we identified and confirmed the characteristics of TOI-5542 through a rigorous analysis of transit signals. TOI-5542 is a relatively dim G-type star exhibiting minimal metallicity and a low rotational speed. Utilizing a combination of radial velocity and astrometric data, we determined that TOI-5542 hosts a massive Jupiter-like exoplanet, designated TOI-5542b, with a mass of 1.15 times that of Jupiter. TOI-5542b completes its orbit around its host star in 161.4 days, with a 3.8-day transit lasting between 1:30 and 2:00 AM. TOI-5542b exhibits a radius of 0.132 Jupiter radii and a derived density of 2.05 g/cm$^3$, suggesting the presence of an extended, low-density atmosphere. TOI-5542 and TOI-5542b are incorporated into our database of massive planets with extended orbits that experience significant orbital precession and dynamical interactions.

We develop an algorithm to solve a convex optimization problem for finite-horizon constrained Markov decision processes (CMDMD). Our algorithm leverages dual random matrix theory to derive the dual problem, which we then formulate as two subproblems. The first subproblem can be efficiently solved using established techniques, while the second is solved via a novel method, resulting in an overall runtime of O(T^(1.25) * k^(1.25) * (T + k)^(1/4) * epsilon^(-2)), where T is the horizon, k is the size of dual variables, and epsilon is the precision. This approach also yields an alternative algorithm with an additional logarithmic factor in the runtime.

This project aims to develop an offline recognition system for handwritten mathematical expressions, building on existing research that focused on handwritten text recognition. By analyzing the structural similarities between text and mathematical expressions, which consist of recognizable units separated by distinct boundaries, we can apply the principles of both offline text and image classification to the problem. Our proposed framework involves a hybrid model that integrates a CNN for feature extraction and an HMM for sequence-based handwriting analysis. Additionally, we develop a specialized keyboard with 115 characters, taking into consideration the expanded set of symbols found in mathematical notation compared to standard text. To further enhance the system, we create an offline alignment tool that synchronizes the sequences with the corresponding image frames and a training module for learning feature mappings and HMM parameters. Our proposed offline recognition pipeline involves initial feature extraction, sequence-based analysis, and combining the results from both HMM and classification layers to generate a final recognized sequence. Our approach has been successfully tested on an offline dataset of mathematical expressions.

We establish a projective F-dimension filtration on the derived category of coherent sheaves 
$\mathbb{Coh}^\bullet(X)$ of a smooth algebraic variety $X$. The lengths of these filiations correspond 
to Euler characteristics of line bundles. It is shown that these filiations on $\mathbb{Coh}^\bullet(X)$ 
can be extended to mixed Dixmier-Douady classes in $H^3(X, \mathbb{Z})$. This class is constructed 
from a supersymmetric quantum system, specifically a sheaf of algebras $\mathcal{A}$ on $X$. 
The construction is analogous to a previous work, but with key differences due to the distinct 
nature of the varieties involved.

Understanding the behavior of interconnected systems relies heavily on analyzing their dynamic relationships, particularly through the concept of Granger causality. This is achieved by examining asymmetric connections within network configurations that are rooted in temporal correlations. These connections are influenced by different types of fluctuations present in processes, which in turn are a result of variations in their temporal characteristics. In this study, we investigate the variability in interactions within networks by generating simulations using coupled non-linear oscillator models with configurable components. Our results reveal networks with consistent fluctuations tend to be robust and stable, whereas those with high variability in fluctuations are susceptible to changes in structure.

Recently, a novel method, known as Maximum Actor-Critic (MAXAC), has emerged in reinforcement learning, shifting the focus from maximizing expected rewards to maximizing the coverage of state-action spaces. Comprising an actor-critic framework with an entropy term, MAXAC's theoretical foundation ensures its ability to achieve unsaturated policies and secure optimal performance in both on-policy and off-policy settings. We introduce a modified MAXAC, termed HMAXAC, by integrating Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) to conduct thorough state-action coverage. In contrast to existing off-policy algorithms that rely on importance sampling, HMAXAC leverages HMC to perform robust exploration. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that HMAXAC outperforms its state-of-the-art counterparts, yielding improved performance and enhanced robustness.
A fundamental proof for the Twin Prime Conjecture has been established.

This research paper proposes the development of a Sonar integration module for a mobile robot, complementing previously described software and hardware setups. Real-time Sonar data is crucial for constructing a comprehensive environment map, enabling the robot to generate feasible trajectories and effectively respond to sudden sonar alerts within real-time constraints.

Our team conducted a thorough examination of Nereid, Saturn's distant moon, by analyzing its reflectance spectrum in the near-infrared range. We identified distinct features that can be attributed to crystalline and amorphous ice, as well as complex dark material. By comparing these observations with those of other Trans-Saturnian Objects, we found similarities in their spectral characteristics. We then used these results to constrain the composition, surface properties, and thermal state of Nereid's surface, as well as to test various formation and evolution hypotheses.

Let $R_n$ be the set of lower triangular matrices of size $n+1$ over a field $F$, with entries from $F[x]/(t^{n+1})$ in the bottom-left corner and identity in the top-right corner. We will now discuss the affine plane denoted as $\mathcal{A}_n$ and the projective plane denoted as $\mathcal{P}_n$, which are constructed based on the ring $R_n$. It's important to note that these planes satisfy a unique property, as they cannot be isomorphic to any plane $\mathcal{A}_k$ or $\mathcal{P}_k$ for any $k \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$.

We examine the impact of specific model properties on the satisfaction level of the statement "Every Tukey-order with models is eventually bounded" in different set-theoretic scenarios. To achieve this, we introduce a novel method for constructing a forcing poset with unique features, which significantly influences the satisfaction of certain principles related to ultrapower orderings with models. This new construction enables us to refine existing results, ultimately leading to a novel forcing notion that facilitates a simpler proof of a key theorem established in a prior study.

A pivotal objective in the field of Operations Research is the creation of context-sensitive decision support systems. Research has shown that the development of such systems is complicated due to the need for contextual information, which is often uncertain. In this study, we focus on the development of Bayesian contextual policy learning algorithms that minimize the risk of suboptimal average regret. Our approach prioritizes the minimization of risks associated with the average regret. We demonstrate that the average regret associated with our proposed algorithms is lower than, or comparable to, those achieved by the standard Q-learning method. Furthermore, our analysis shows the effectiveness of the Bayesian algorithms in the areas of kidney exchange and electricity load forecasting.

To establish a resdual vector space framework, we need to redefine the dual vector space. This new definition enables us to prove that it reverses certain categorical relationships between linear algebraic structures. As a result, we can naturally restore pre-dualities that were previously forced by this old definition, which now shows it has several disadvantages. Using this natural dualism, we can also restore pre-dualities for spaces and measures, which shows measures are essentially the dual of probabilities. This allows us to prove key results like the Gelfand-Naymark representation theorem, which shows any bounded linear functional on a space of integrable functions can be represented as an integrable function.

A recent proof by Spekkins showed that one can model a simple version of quantum behavior, even simpler than the Hiley-Mickleman system, using a set of 240 lines within a 8-dimensional space of whole number coordinates. This is achieved by using whole number coordinates to represent elements of a symmetry group known as E8. However, it's also possible to model all quantum properties by using the whole number coordinate space of $E_8$, which is composed of 240 specific points within that space. By applying the rules of quantum mechanics to these coordinates directly, we can derive the standard quantum rules for measurements and find that all contextuality and entanglement tests are satisfied as expected in quantum mechanics. This derivation provides a clear and straightforward way to apply quantum rules and may give insights into the fundamental structure of quantum theory as well.

We suggest that a homogeneous superconducting state with complex ordering parameters characterized by quasi-momentum can arise when the momentum dependence of the critical temperature is influenced by a non-trivial Berry phase in the underlying single-particle Hamiltonian. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent in systems exhibiting non-trivial topological properties in their electronic band structure. Given that a specific phase is inextricably linked to topological bands, it must be a continuous value. Consequently, any non-trivial topological feature is characterized by an integer representation of this continuous value, which must hold true for the phase itself as well. Consequently, the phase must exhibit singularities that are associated with defects in the system, which manifest as vortices within the superconducting material, where their distribution is directly related to the topological properties of the system, even in the absence of an external magnetic field, leading to unique characteristics such as the presence of circulating currents and a modified energy spectrum of the electrons.

We have established a framework for examining the topological properties of linked groups by studying the topological characteristics of their individual components and a key subgroup that determines their structure. The investigation focuses on the behavior of compact and connected components, as well as the free rank of the quotient groups obtained from the Abelian groups in question. Specifically, we have derived a criterion for determining the local compactness of a linked group based on properties of its constituent parts. The study also examines the conditions under which a specific type of quotient, known as the Torus, appears in the theory. The main results have been generalized to include the study of linked groups of any given complexity.

Presence-absence data is commonly encountered in numerous research areas, particularly in taxonomy, ecology, and linguistics. Although various distance measures and clustering techniques are available, their effectiveness has not been thoroughly evaluated for high-dimensional binary data. This research aims to fill this gap by comparing the performance of different algorithms using high-dimensional synthetic data sets containing presence-absence variables. We specifically examine the impact of data generation processes on the results, considering scenarios where established methods excel in traditional settings but may fail in novel situations.

In recent years, deep neural networks have significantly advanced the field of salient object detection, yet network architecture design and training methods continue to be areas for improvement. This paper introduces a comprehensive and cohesive approach for designing novel, high-performance networks and develops two innovative structures, either of which can enhance the networks' capabilities. Furthermore, a novel training method is proposed to enhance the performance of the models. Lastly, extensive experiments were conducted to validate the proposed framework, resulting in outstanding performance across multiple prominent datasets, both with and without depth information.

The UM-IU@LING system for the SemEval-2019 task on detecting abusive language on social media has won first place by combining two distinct models. This strategy involved using BERT to create effective features and training both a linear SVM and a non-linear SVM on those features. A carefully curated dataset of 10,733 English tweets was assembled to fine-tune the BERT model, which was then used to generate features for 20,000 test tweets. These features were subsequently fed into the SVM models to predict the severity of aggression in those tweets. By separating this approach into two parts, we were able to outperform many other solutions at the specified test set metrics of accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and the LogLoss metric.

This paper delves into the relationships between the ratios of adjacent numbers within sequences formed by combining powers of $x$ with their reverses, examining cases where the ratio of consecutive terms equates to $\pm x^{k-l}$. We also provide illustrative examples for each type of sequence and discuss generating sequences that satisfy this criterion.

Computed tomography (CT) scans can be enhanced by using CT detectors with multiple energy levels, yet this technology faces a challenge when dealing with noisy data from lower energy sources. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative approach within a non-linear optimization framework, in which a prior reconstruction is imposed on both the object being scanned and the data obtained from low-energy detectors. A specific model, based on semi-discrete ray tracing, accurately represents the data collected by low- and high-energy detectors, enabling us to jointly optimize both the object and detector denoising. Our model, which incorporates energy-binning variables, proves capable of handling detector noise while also decomposing the object into its constituent materials. We have successfully applied the model to a three-dimensional dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in a full simulation.

Significant advancements in handwritten text recognition (HTR) have been achieved thanks to the availability of large, diverse datasets. However, rare historical languages and languages with limited digital presence lack similar resources, making it difficult to apply standard HTR methods. This paper presents a novel approach to overcome this challenge by introducing an innovative dataset generation technique that utilizes under-resourced handwritten historical documents as a foundation for training a character-level recurrent neural network (RNN). The generated dataset can then be used for HTR tasks despite potential inaccuracies in the generated text labels, which are mitigated through the incorporation of task-specific decoder layers that fine-tune the RNN's output. Experimental evaluations on semi-colar tasks involving Greek and Basque demonstrate that the proposed method can achieve satisfactory results and accurately transcribe previously unseen text.

Heavy elements beyond calcium have been experimentally studied for decades, with a focus on understanding their unique nuclear properties. The application of ab initio theory to these elements has been limited due to the extensive number of particles involved and the rapid growth of computational costs. The inclusion of excitations further exacerbates this challenge. The inclusion of these factors has made ab initio calculations intractable. A major breakthrough occurred in 2021, when a breakthrough enabled ab initio calculations of key nuclei, marking a significant milestone. The inclusion of these factors has made subsequent calculations a realistic possibility. The inclusion of these factors has made subsequent calculations a realistic possibility. The inclusion of these factors has made subsequent calculations a realistic possibility.

We begin to understand the principles of one-dimensional topological phases by examining the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where we connect edge mode appearances to specific model features, relating them to the concept of effective momentum and topological charge. Building on this foundation, we use the model to introduce learners to advanced concepts such as Berry phase, Chern number, and topological insulators, also considering a variation of the model with spin-orbit coupling that can generate mid-edge states.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain types of convex domains in complex plane pairs. These specific areas include polygons with more than three vertices, specific convex discs generated by analytic curves, and domains shaped like rectangles, circles, triangles, and ellipses.

We establish the finiteness of two-loop four-point amplitudes in anti-de Sitter space within supersymmetric gravity, specifically bordering on unitarity, by employing scalar-photon duality. This approach allows us to rewrite gravity amplitudes in terms of lower-dimensional field theory data, facilitating calculations through established field-theoretic methods. The connection to field theory also enables us to pinpoint and eliminate divergences in the amplitude calculations, ultimately rendering them finite. The employed duality, when applied to $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity, leaves one divergence unresolved, suggesting potential avenues for resolving the issue through incorporating zeta-function regularity principles, thereby enhancing the relationship between the two theories.

The rapid growth of GPU capabilities has made them the preferred choice for accelerating computationally intensive tasks. However, most GPU allocators are based on byte-level, which is insufficient for data types that require alignment and endianness. This limitation hinders the full potential of GPUs in cooperative object-based programming. Our research introduces a new object-level GPU memory allocator called DynaSOAr, specifically designed for the NVIDIA Tesla Dalian accelerator. By leveraging the precise addressing capabilities of DynaSOAr, cooperative object-based programs can achieve better performance. Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms the standard CUDA allocator in terms of CPU-GPU data transfer, while also achieving comparable performance in CPU-GPU data exchange. Additionally, DynaSOAr enables better locality and minimizes the overhead of page tables.

A wide range of minimal Standard Model extensions with one additional gauge symmetry is explored in this study, from the minimal $U(1)_X$ model to $U(1)_{B-L}$ and $U(1)_{P}$. These models are based on the parent groups $SU(5) \times U(1)_{a}$, $SU(6)$, and $SO(10)$, and their properties and relationships are examined. Distinguishing features and predictions of these models are identified, and constraints on their parameters are discussed in the context of electroweak symmetry breaking, flavor physics, and gauge coupling unification. The analysis also includes the implications of anomaly mediation for low-energy supersymmetry and the effects of additional Higgs doublets in these models. The study is accompanied by two appendices, focusing on the Higgs sector and a summary of $U(1)$ charge assignments.

Understanding the behavior of pressurized biological tubes, such as those involved in cell migration, requires in-depth analysis of their tube model. Research has shown that the ends of these cantilevered tubes experience tension, affecting their mechanical stability. However, existing studies on the tube model have not fully explained the source of the tension at their ends. This knowledge gap hinders our understanding of the mechanical properties of migrating cells. Our study fills this void by presenting a new theoretical framework based on a pressurized cane structure, allowing us to develop an analytical model that accurately describes the tension and stability of the tubes. Our research reveals that the axial tension at the ends of the tubes is directly related to their radius and internal pressure and can be experimentally verified. Moreover, we found that increasing internal pressure can stabilize clamped, but not pinned, beams under compressive loads. The implications of our work are far-reaching, as they enable us to better understand the mechanical properties of cells and their ability to migrate through various tissues.

In safety-critical applications, ensuring the reliability of classifiers is essential.
Traditional classifiers depend on precise assumptions, which are often not met in real-world data, leading to unreliable predictions.
To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework for training robust credal Bayesian networks using an efficient constraint relaxation technique over probabilistic circuits.
This framework allows us to train classifiers that are guaranteed to maintain a minimum accuracy rate even in the presence of adversarial perturbations.

Initially proposed in 1925, Bloch oscillations have been challenging to detect experimentally for nearly nine decades. This difficulty stems from diffusive disorder and interactions with phonons in solid-state systems, but researchers have now overcome this obstacle in ultrasonics. A new study demonstrates experimentally and theoretically how to achieve and identify Bloch oscillations using active, sound-waving slabs made of separate sound sources. By using this approach, the team was able to observe acceleration, velocity, and deceleration, which correspond to different stages of Bloch oscillations. Furthermore, they demonstrated the ability to control the process using an enhanced ultrasonic grating. This breakthrough paves the way for applying the concept of Bloch oscillations in diverse fields, from photonics to phononics and even semiconductors.

This research introduces and investigates a code property, to a neighbour, in symmetry, on a point code in a generalised quadrangle. Specifically, a neighbour- and point-code symmetry property is established and demonstrated to be sufficient for expanding the code into a code distribution over the entire space. Furthermore, this is related to expanding partial spreads to total spreads. The study considers specific cases within certain generalised quadrangles and provides several examples of new and previously known neighbour- and point-invariant codes in various quadrangle types. Ultimately, the study presents a conjecture that essentially states a question about the minimum weight of a 1-neighbour-invariant code in a specific quadrangle.

Our team conducted a thorough examination of the anomaly in the 2D correlation function of the GCMBD survey, focusing on its unusual anisotropy. By utilizing a sophisticated anisotropic ellipsoid model, we were able to accurately fit the data and quantify the anisotropy's impact. We identified that anisotropy significantly influences two-point correlations at small scales, influencing their direction and structure. This study's findings also indicate that anisotropy is not only prevalent in the CMZ but is present in various environments, including the VCMB, GC, and BCMB. We found that anisotropy is influenced by factors such as distance and spatial orientation. Moreover, we discovered that anisotropy is present in other regions of the GCMBD survey, including the VCMB, GC, and BCMB. This is the first time anisotropy has been comprehensively studied in the GCMBD survey data, and our results provide a detailed understanding of its prevalence and impact.

This research presents a straightforward model describing the temporal evolution of electron groups following X-ray absorption in solids. The findings indicate that high-intensity X-ray pulses can alter a solid's electronic and atomic structure, causing its absorption spectrum to deviate from normal low-intensity XANES. Consequently, the sample may appear to lose certain atoms. To address this issue, we present a rate-based electron absorption model validated through first-principles calculations and experiments on ZnO, with a typical accuracy of within 10%.

A CMOS-based, on-chip temperature sensor has been developed, utilizing an advanced BCMS process. The proposed sensor is both energy-efficient and low-cost, operating within a supply voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V. A bandgap reference circuit is employed to produce a temperature-dependent voltage. The resulting voltage is then converted to a digital format using a successive-approximation register analog-to-digital converter. The designed sensor exhibits a remarkable 0.24{\deg}C resolution and an operational temperature span of 25{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C. Furthermore, the on-chip temperature sensor achieves a competitive energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion, while also demonstrating a strong agreement between simulated and measured results.

A key process in quantum information is generating high-quality entangled photons. 
We've developed an efficient method to create entangled photons by combining two
degenerate quantum scissors circuits, which is a method of deleting a photon from a specific mode. 
Due to the non-deterministic nature of this process, our approach is also non-deterministic in generating entanglement. 
However, unlike other methods, it relies on a different principle – post-selection instead of post-measurement. 
We'll demonstrate the entanglement produced by this method using the correlation coefficient and various measures of quantumness. 
Experimental results show that the achieved fidelity exceeds the maximum possible with classical means. 
The study also identifies the primary sources of error, which are the addition process imperfections and losses within the optical setup. 
The non-deterministic entanglement creation method could be utilized in scenarios requiring sub-optimal success rates but offering superior quality.

In the unit disk graph model, we introduce two algorithms for creating nearly Euclidean spanners, one for fixed and another for dynamically increasing freedom. Our algorithms yield sparsely composed structures, with the first having O(F^(1+epsilon)) edges and the second having O(F log^(1/2)(F) log log(F) / epsilon^2) edges, thus improving existing disk functionality algorithms by providing better bounds and generalizing results to a broader range of freedom levels.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in using machine learning to categorize IoT devices based on their response to probing requests. Our research focuses on reducing the costs associated with probing while maintaining accurate feature sets. We developed an adaptive method for selecting the cheapest subsets of features from a dynamic pool of options, utilizing a binary program to optimize device classification. Since resolving this problem is NP-hard, we created an efficient heuristic approach, which we tested using a realistic dataset of IoT devices, along with various existing feature selection techniques and an optimized feature subset selection method.

We examine the semantic properties of Goedel modal logic along with its extensions, notably Intuitionistic and Grishin modal logics. Correspondingly, we analyze algebraic structures, specifically Goedel algebras with additional operators. We then establish a dual equivalence between the categories of Goedel spaces (etc.) and their respective algebraic counterparts (etc. ), effectively bridging modal logic traditions with the study of ordered algebraic structures such as Hoops and lattices.

This research explores a novel method for improving machine translation and word alignment processes by leveraging outside data beyond standard parallel corpora. We developed a system that utilizes a large, publicly available English-German dictionary to enhance the performance of the FastAlign algorithm. Our experiments on the IWSLT machine translation system and the mTEC text collection showed significant improvements in the system's BLEU score and the precision of the word alignment process. The novel method also had the added benefit of reducing the required training data by 50% without compromising performance. We further analyzed the effect of this new resource on the accuracy of specific, challenging word pair alignments.

This paper presents a distinct algorithm for building Nash equilibria in a finite game with multiple players. The algorithm's optimality relies on the convexity of the space containing mixed strategies. Using this strategy, we convert the problem of establishing mixed strategy equilibria into the problem of finding zeros for certain functions. We demonstrate through numerical examples that constructing Nash equilibria via this algorithm may yield multiple solutions, each representing a different level of accuracy for the final equilibrium. The efficiency of the algorithm's convergence is heavily influenced by the choice of starting point.

By analyzing the stellar population's impact on final stellar mass, we calculated the steepest mass loss function possible. We utilized PopSyCLE to simulate a mass loss function that causes 90% of stars to lose mass during supernova explosions. We then investigated the conditions under which these objects could form and survive to the present day as primordial black holes. We simulated objects with masses ranging from 0.1 to 1000 solar masses and found that our aggressive mass loss scenario significantly reduces the required conditions for these objects to exist today. We compared our findings with the most conservative mass loss scenario and observed a substantial discrepancy, particularly for lower mass objects. We also calculated the rate of objects within our mass window and found that our aggressive mass loss scenario results in a substantial decrease in this rate. We further examined the implications of our results on the detection of dark matter through indirect detection methods, such as gamma-ray emissions from matter accretion by these objects.

Research into the behavior of complex molecules, particularly those that resemble a combination of spheres and wedges, has been limited to computational studies. This research investigates the crystalline structures of molecules consisting of a hard sphere and a wedge-shaped cap by simulating the effects of both internal and external forces. By varying the angle of the wedge-shaped caps and measuring the critical point at which the molecules transition between liquid and solid states, the team found the critical angle to be 60.5 degrees, consistent with previous studies. Results from the simulations showed the liquid-solid transition is characterized by a unique modulated structure, where the crystalline pattern exhibits a distinct wave-like formation. Furthermore, the team discovered a second transition, where the modulated structure transforms into a more complex, multi-layered lattice as the temperature decreases. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of complex molecules, with potential applications in the design of new materials.

The researchers in this work derived stochastic field equations that stop changing at specific times, similar to the time-constrained condition in the heat equation, and derived from the Wiener process at those stagnation times. They established two main equations: a primary equation and a secondary, and then derived and verified their consistency. Similarities were noted with the space-based Poisson and Laplace equations as well as their stochastic equivalents, which led to new solutions for field models that relate to the sphere's geometry and geometries with constant positive or negative curvature. Additionally, certain class members from one of the models found here and previously studied in another paper have specific geometrical characteristics. Furthermore, certain solutions of one of the models found here and previously studied in another paper have specific geometrical characteristics.

We have developed and experimentally demonstrated a newly formulated protocol for observing the spatial distribution of an object using photons that do not interact with it. Our implementation builds on the principles of the Heisenberg interferometer and leverages the detection of a secondary set of photons to "imprint" measurement information, effectively enabling the holographic reconstruction of an object from a primary group of photons that remain undetected. Our results align with those from prior computational studies and demonstrate a significant advancement in quantum imaging technology, offering the potential for detecting delicate samples, such as those found in biological applications.

The flow resistance, or friction, experienced by fluids as they move through complex structures, such as the surfaces of foams, has been an area of study for nearly a century. By using high-speed cameras to observe the flow of gas through a foam with a channel that can be changed in texture, or pattern, or shape, researchers have found that irregularities in the foam's surface significantly affect its resistance. In addition to their unique shape, other factors such as the size of the bubbles and the type of fluid also influence friction. Notably, the position of the foam within the channel plays a crucial role in determining friction levels at very low speeds. Furthermore, the way that the foam's structure changes as it moves through the channel can be used to predict its friction coefficient.

This study addresses the challenges posed by data imbalance and diversity in medical image analysis for skin cancer diagnosis. A novel method is introduced, combining the method of entropies of decision with a pre-trained VGG16 network. By analyzing the uncertainty of the pre-trained model's classification decisions across multiple datasets, pre-defined outlier samples are identified. These samples are then used to fine-tune the pre-trained model and to retrain a new classification network. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving accurate skin cancer diagnosis.

We've developed a novel, ultrafast and precise method for measuring the thermal relaxation of free electrons in sodium. Sodium's simple electronic structure enables highly accurate theoretical predictions. Our experiments involve heating sodium electrons using its photoexcitation cross-section, with the thermal density perturbation response being amenable to both precise measurement via optical reflectivity and theoretical prediction through ab-initu many-body quantum theory. Our results in the visible spectrum reveal that the electron density fluctuation is governed by free-carrier Drude dispersion, with the electron-electron interaction dominating thermal relaxation for thin film depths up to approximately 10 nm. Our findings align with advanced quantum Monte Carlo calculations. Conversely, ion recovery processes, governed by electron-phonon interaction, become the dominant energy dissipation mechanism at greater depths.

Ensemble theory's fundamental principle is that time and space averages are equivalent, 
but this assumption breaks down when the phase space volume changes as it does in non-conservative systems.
To prevent this issue, a solution involves utilizing trajectories generated through Hamiltonian extensions of non-conservative forces.
Another critical premise for ensemble theory to be valid is that all microstates are equally probable, 
but this assumption fails in cases such as the free expansion where the phase space volume is dynamic.
A novel method has been developed to rectify such instances by applying a corrective factor to the probability measure of microstates, 
effectively counteracting the phase space change. The proposed correction involves multiplying the standard Gibbs measure by an exponential of the Hamiltonian.

Calculation of the Kontsevich weights of graphs representing connections and curvatures for quadratic (symplectic) Poisson structures is addressed. This calculation was a key component in C. Menichi's proof of the Euler characteristic being zero for closed orientable surfaces with such structures. Given an arbitrary symplectic Poisson structure on a manifold, its local expression can be written in a coordinate system as $(\pi^{ij}(x) = (\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}, \ldots, \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_n})$. This allows the definition of a symplectic Frobenius algebra structure on the vector space $V$, spanned by $e_1, \ldots, e_n$, with a symmetric invariant bilinear form $B$, a commutative multiplication $m$, and a non-degenerate skew-symmetric form $C$, representing the symplectic matrix $\pi(x_o)$ at a point $x_o$. This representation, along with a set of graph invariants, facilitates the expansion of $\pi^{ij}(x)$ in terms of $x_i, x_j$ and their curvatures using the given form. This connection is represented by certain graphs called $\pi$ and $C$, whose weights form a set of invariants that can be calculated.

This work investigates localized waves in the Ginzburg-Landau equation on a curved surface with negative curvature, representing the curvature of a trampoline. The equation is modified with two small parameters, allowing for a zone of interaction where the curvature effects and the non-linear effects are balanced. Under these conditions, solutions known as nanoptera can emerge. The first set of nanoptera consists of primary peaks accompanied by secondary peaks in the distance, controlled by an exponential factor. The amplitude of the primary peak is connected to the amplitude of the secondary peaks through a relationship that is linearly dependent on an exponential factor. The peaks' distances are also related to each other through another exponential factor. We have found two types of stable nanoptera solutions, each with its own unique relationship between the amplitudes and distances of the primary and secondary peaks. One type of stable nanoptera solution has a real-valued relationship between the amplitudes and distances of the primary and secondary peaks, while the other type of stable nanoptera solution has a complex-valued relationship between the amplitudes and distances of the primary and secondary peaks. We have found that the amplitudes and distances of the secondary peaks are controlled by parameters that are independent of the small parameters of the system. These findings are relevant to the study of localized waves in the context of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the Klein-Gordon equation and other systems.

Non-Gaussian characteristics of meta-invariant modes in a multi-field inflation scenario can offer a window into the inflaton's fluctuations beyond the horizon. This capability stems from the influence of these long-lived fluctuations on the trajectory of inflation, resulting in the distortion of some cosmological signals. This phenomenon is analogous to the cosmological collider effect, which amplifies massive spin states through resonance. While the collider effect is generally confined to sub-horizon scales, its imprint is detectable within long-wavelength modes. This research investigates whether the signal produced by the collider effect can be discerned within a single, long-wavelength mode. This is feasible given that this mode can undergo multiple transformations and thus retain multiple signals. This is particularly applicable to skewness, whose signal pattern is more intricate than that of the tree-level bispectrum. This study demonstrates that a heavy field trajectory, induced by interactions with multiple massless fields, can generate a skewness signal consistent with the predicted pattern of the trispectrum. This consistency is evident in simulations of inflation models featuring particles heavy relative to the Hubble scale but coupled through an intermediate massless state. This consistency arises from the meta-invariant long-wavelength mode modulation, which remains unaffected by the Hubble rate. This feature is shared with the tree-level bispectrum, which is why both are termed "pristine features."

WeAcC is an constructed family of graphs called accordion graphs, specifically C(2m,n), which is a type of semi-symmetric graph with a degree of four. The AcC pairings, a perfect matching of pairs of vertices in C(2m,n), are established and identified. The conditions under which accordion graphs are hamiltonian or traceable are determined. Additionally, the C(2m,n) graph is found to be isomorphic to a type of quartic circulant graph known as (a,b)(c,d)(e,f)(g,h)(i,j). The conditions for this isomorphism are established and identified.

We investigate one- and two-dimensional quantum walks with anyon anyonic statistics, focusing on three-state qudits. By analyzing the spreading of the walk's probability distribution, we find power-law scaling laws for global dynamical measures, such as the first and second moments. In the one-dimensional case, our results align with known ballistic and sub-ballistic behaviors. In the two-dimensional scenario, our findings are consistent with a generally ballistic behavior, with an exception for when the spin quantum number is one, in which case we observe a transition to a diffusive phase.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning (SSL) have enabled models to achieve exceptional performance in unsupervised settings, yet their internal feature representations remain poorly understood. Leveraging a cluster-level contrastive learning objective, our study delves into the characteristics of SSL transformer (SSL-T) tiered features in response to various image transformations. Through empirical evidence, we found that higher-level features tend to capture task-relevant semantic information, a phenomenon particularly pronounced when using self-supervised transformers. Moreover, we discovered that incorporating momentum encoder warmup and a starter weight initialization can enhance the emerging attributes of MoCo, thereby improving its transferability to downstream tasks without necessitating additional supervised fine-tuning. Our findings are substantiated when using downstream tasks that require fine-grained semantic understanding, showcasing the utility of our proposed techniques.

The standard $\Lambda$CDM model is an excellent fit for current cosmological data, but its theoretical underpinnings are flawed due to the irreconcilable difference between dark energy and dark matter. Researchers have developed various models of unified dark substance (UDS) to address this incompatibility, but most assume a direct proportionality between the energy densities of the dark components, which contradicts observational data. Researchers have developed a novel model of UDS based on quantum field theory, incorporating non-conservation of particle number and a Drude model for the vacuum, in an attempt to reconcile the dark energy and dark matter compatibility issue and their observational inconsistencies.

A simple, direct proof of a specific theorem regarding incompressible Euler equations has been established. This proof validates that certain Sobolev space applications of the theorem are indeed problematic or incorrect.

In recent years, text-to-image diffusion models have become increasingly popular, yet fully controlling their generated images through prompt engineering alone remains challenging, particularly when it comes to subtle details. While diffusion guidance techniques aim to bridge this gap, they often require altering the underlying model architecture or training process, which limits their broad applicability. Our research introduces "The Stable Creator," a universal plugin that enhances the inferencing stage of pre-trained diffusion models to expand their controllable generation capabilities. Our approach leverages the pre-trained Stable Diffusion model, supplementing it with an extra U-Net and a Set of Control-Words-Encoder to enable management of specific concepts such as stability, artistic style, or level of detail. Our experimentally validated The Stable Creator can be seamlessly applied to various pre-trained diffusion models and significantly enhances user control, surpassing existing methods by a substantial 20% in accuracy according to our evaluation. Our code is freely available at https://github.com/alexandervanhees/stable-creator.

A significant hurdle in signal processing is the issue of forward and backward ambiguity, particularly in the context of reversible data hiding where multiple patterns can be generated from the original signal after embedding. A new approach utilizing a recurrent neural network, trained in a Bayesian manner, has been proposed to predict the most suitable image block for the given watermarked signal and current hidden bit. By leveraging the uncertainty in Bayesian neural networks, the network can provide confidence levels in its predictions, enabling the original signal and candidate watermarked signals to be ranked according to the most likely original image. By utilizing the predictions from RNebayes along with a basic thresholding method, the quality of reconstructed signal after extraction is enhanced, and the improved performance is demonstrated through simulation results.

Our investigation focuses on the chiral effective field theory for light neutrinos and dark matter. We propose a $J/\psi$ decay channel that is consistent with this framework and could potentially be observed experimentally. By conducting a detailed analysis of $J/\psi$ decays to various final states, we determine the associated effective interactions and estimate their magnitude, ultimately estimating a lower bound on the mediator mass in these interactions.

High-resolution observations of the solar chromosphere are limited by current instrumentation, which hinders the exploration of the solar chromosphere's environment below the transition region and its connection to the solar magnetic field type. A study utilizing the HiRISE instrument on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter on Mars examines the properties of small, bright solar features from the surface of the sun, which are unaffected by the transition region. By analyzing these features, the study provides a foundation for future investigations into the chromosphere's magnetic environment using future instruments such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope. Data from 1000 bright solar spots were examined, and initial findings indicate distinct morphological characteristics for each type of solar magnetic field, with one type exhibiting smaller features with higher motion variability, and the other type exhibiting fewer, larger features with lower variability.

Human vision is an incredibly complex and energy-intensive process, making it difficult to replicate with current technology. In contrast, the way the brain processes visual information is both energy-efficient and fast. Films, on the other hand, are relatively simple to create and consume, yet they have the power to convey profound messages and evoke emotional responses. Interestingly, there's a growing trend in the realm of digital art, known as minimal films, which are becoming an area of interest for researchers in the field of dynamic recognition. These films, characterized by their simplicity and the absence of excessive special effects, can be analyzed and understood frame by frame, providing valuable insights into the capabilities of the human visual system and the principles of dynamic recognition.

If dark matter consists of galactic magnetic Monopoles with extremely long lifetimes, there should be some of them present in our galaxy today. These dark monopoles would interact with our galaxy's magnetic fields, and those fields have a non-zero average strength. This means our galaxy's overall magnetic energy cannot be zero, indicating a fundamental difference between ordinary and dark matter in how they contribute to the galaxy's matter content.

This work introduces a new deep learning model called ClimateFormer, designed to predict future weather patterns using numerical numerical weather modeling model outputs. Building on the success of the transformer model in computer vision, particularly its success in predicting the movement of objects over time, we demonstrate its applicability to weather forecasting. To address the issue of increased computation due to considering the entire weather map at once, we present a novel hybrid model combining the benefits of self-attention and a new cross-attention mechanism that breaks the weather map into separate areas. This approach retains long-range dependencies between different regions while significantly reducing computation. We also introduce a new technique called progressive patch expansion, which allows the model to learn the forecast process step-by-step. This results in a model that outperforms current alternatives in predicting weather patterns with only a fraction of the required computation.

We propose a novel class of dark matter models based on the three-Higgs-doublet model with $S_3$ discrete symmetry, resulting in one dark matter candidate being protected from one-loop corrections by the model's symmetry, while the other candidate is the Lightest Stable Particle (LSP) capable of receiving significant boosts from additional tree-level contributions to the dark matter annihilation rate.

A particular class of multipartite quantum states, known as quads, can be partitioned into distinct binary subsets, each comprising entangled states, yet their collective sum, when normalized, forms bounded entanglement. We identify a unique form of quads, specific to binary systems, formed by entangling distinct subsets of multipartite quantum states, each within the family of semidefinite fractional permutations. It is demonstrated that all members of this category exhibit PPT entanglement for any prime dimension up to a certain dimension, denoted as $d\leq 17$. Furthermore, a newly discovered PPT entangled binary subset is reported within the family of W permutations.

In the field of mathematical biology, modeling and analyzing complex biological systems is a crucial approach. Focusing on neurons, researchers have developed an optimal control model that uses mathematics to predict the behavior of microtubule transport systems. By applying fundamental biological principles, the model incorporates parameters that are easy to understand from a biological perspective. When simplified, it reduces to a well-known equation for diffusive transport. However, due to the optimal control nature of the model, it can also capture the occurrence of traffic jams in diffusive systems. Utilizing this model, researchers have studied the impact of microtubule regulation on the system and found that an optimal regulation strategy can prevent traffic jams. The research was conducted through an initial value problem formulation, for which an existence and uniqueness theorem was proven, along with a related optimization problem. Further, the study of the optimization problem involved finding necessary conditions for optimality and proving the problem's regularity. The results have been validated through numerical simulations, demonstrating the model's ability to capture both diffusive and jammed transport dynamics.

Financial networks consist of interconnected companies, influencing one another through various transactions. A recent research approach involves analyzing financial networks as graphs, identifying hidden patterns known as network motifs to understand the underlying relationships. These motifs consist of small, recurring graph structures that can provide valuable insights into the financial market's dynamics. An algorithm has been developed to efficiently identify all network motifs, which is then applied to two real-world financial networks - the stock market and business intercorrelations. Furthermore, the study explores how the network's topology can be analyzed using motif frequencies and demonstrates the impact of removing major nodes, such as those corresponding to highly influential companies, on network stability.

In the event of a binary system consisting of a binary star and a supermassive black hole merging, the stellar companion is expected to be disrupted at the point of the black hole's tidal radius, resulting in an accretion disk formation and the emission of high-energy radiation. This study involves numerical simulations to analyze the accretion disk's behavior and the associated emissions resulting from a binary star falling into a black hole with a spin parameter of 0.7. The results reveal that the accretion disk can persist for up to 1000 orbits, with the possibility of reformation after initial fragmentation. The energy released during a black hole merger is found to be 10 to 1000 times greater than typical active galactic nuclei, with the accretion disk's temperature reaching up to 10 to the 6th Kelvin. The energy emitted is primarily in the form of X-rays and gamma-rays, whereas the accretion disk's outer regions emit primarily in the form of ultraviolet radiation. This type of event is predicted to occur at a rate of 10 to 1000 times per galaxy over the lifetime of the galaxy, with the potential to be detected by the e-PTOLEMY telescope.

Three-body semileptonic tau decays serve as a useful tool for investigating hadronic currents and form factors. However, their complexity arises from non-trivial dynamics, making the extraction of individual current components and form factors difficult. A proposed method to isolate these components involves selecting specific kinematic configurations where the form factors are interrelated or negligible. The paper examines the constraints imposed by helicity arguments on three-body weak decays, aiming to identify configurations suitable for experimental study. Additionally, it provides a set of normalized currents and form factors for tau particle calculations.

We've identified a parametric relationship between the Jaccard distance and a generalized measure of normalized information distance, derived in a study by Ferragina and Index, by combining non-empty set cardinalities and the size of their intersection. This parametric family, characterized by two variables $\alpha$ and $\beta$, allows for the exploration of different metric properties. By setting $\alpha$ and $\beta$ to different values, we've found that it's possible to obtain valid metrics, effectively bridging the gap between the Jaccard distance and the original Tversky similarity. By choosing specific values for $\alpha$ (between 0 and 1) and setting $\beta$ to 1, we've found that it's possible to obtain valid metric properties, thereby expanding our understanding of the Jaccard distance and its applications.

Our proposed approach, Motion De-blurring (MDP), tackles the challenge of non-uniform de-blurring for both human figures and complex backgrounds. Current methods often struggle with de-blurring complex scenes due to the difficulty in accurately modeling long-range dependencies, which our approach aims to address by jointly blurring and de-blurring the entire image. By building on the success of RetinexNet in separating complex backgrounds into distinct components, our method focuses on directly targeting the motion-blurred human subject. This is achieved through the use of two modules, which introduce controlled blur and restore the original image, respectively. Our approach's motion restoration module is designed to be component-agnostic, allowing it to effectively reconstruct the original complex scene from the independently retinex-separated components. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on publicly available datasets, which show that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art de-blurring techniques in terms of overall performance. Additionally, our qualitative analysis reveals that our approach excels in de-blurring a wide range of complex scenes.

Inspired by the adaptability and resilience of neural networks, we propose a groundbreaking approach to create adaptive and fault-tolerant computer circuits at the molecular level, utilizing self-assembling chemical reactions. Our methodology employs a universal programming system based on DNA's self-assembly capabilities to build artificial spiking neurons that operate through chemical reactions. We successfully constructed a functional neuron and simulated its learning process, capturing key characteristics of biological neurons, such as plasticity and complex network behaviors. Furthermore, our approach enables the creation of complex, adaptive systems that can be reprogrammed for different tasks.

This article serves two main purposes: first, a specific type of infinite sequence, known as an interval chain of type $(\kappa,\lambda)$, is defined and its fundamental properties examined; second, an essential characteristic of the ultrapower generated by a poset $P$ is investigated, specifically whether every interval type within the poset is preserved in the ultrapower, leading to the introduction of properties $D_\kappa$ and $E_\kappa$ for filters on the poset.

Preprocessing is a crucial initial step in any data analysis process, aimed at converting raw data into a suitable format for further examination. The preprocessing step is characterized by several common operations, such as data normalization, splitting, and handling missing values, which are typically described in general terms. However, each dataset has its own unique requirements, necessitating a more tailored approach to preprocessing. A proposed framework for profiling allows researchers to customize their strategies based on the specific characteristics of the data at hand, including the identification of the data type, the presence of noise, and the encoding method. By integrating a set of predefined data transformation rules, the framework can automate the preprocessing step, thereby streamlining the process and reducing the likelihood of errors. Our dataset profiling framework was successfully tested on 2000 samples drawn from 162 datasets, yielding promising results.

A main goal in understanding Hadwiger's conjecture is to examine how the chromatic number of a minimal complete graph contraction relates to the original graph's coloring. A specific type of contraction, the tree plus contraction, restricts the original graph's sparsity structure. This relation leads to two main findings: (1) a proof that any minimal $k$-chromatic graph contracted from a tree has a $k-1$-coloring, and (2 a proof that any minimal 5-chromatic graph contracted from a tree has a specific substructure that indicates a 6-coloring.

This research paper introduces an innovative approach for reconstructing sparse signals from graph-based representations, utilizing an adaptive Correntropy-based Probabilistic Prior (CAPP) that corresponds to the Exponential Euclidean Distance (EE Distance). A novel form of EE Distance is developed and its equivalence to the generalized correntropy is demonstrated. Furthermore, a kernel width is dynamically adjusted to maximize the likelihood of observing residual errors. The proposed method effectively minimizes the negative log-likelihood of the observation error under the CAPP, thereby yielding a computationally efficient algorithm. This new approach is then applied to address the issue of sparse graph signal denoising, yielding a correspondance with the Maximum Absolute Error (MAE) optimization principle. Under certain circumstances, the proposed algorithm converges rapidly, resulting in Correntropy Minimization (CM) of the residual errors. The performance of the proposed method is then evaluated through numerical experiments, showcasing its superior noise robustness and precise reconstruction of the underlying graph signal.

In a recent experiment involving a spinor BEC, researchers detected signatures of atom-phonon interactions lasting only about 100 milliseconds due to environmental noise from the detector. Our study develops a theoretical framework based on optimal state generation and quantum amplitude amplification to extend this noise-free time frame. By applying a precise magnetic field sequence, we create entangled spin states and apply an operator that gradually changes the spin population, effectively applying a 'rotation' in the system. We apply the inverse of this operation a certain number of times to maximize the production of a particular spin state, and our results show that the number of iterations needed to produce an almost pure anti-aligned state is relatively small.

This research focuses on estimating the initial eigenvalue for a nonlinear eigenvalue problem that arises from an isotropic, nonlinear differential equation within a bounded area, subject to a specific boundary condition. By defining a specific function related to the given differential equation, we establish a precise lower bound for this eigenvalue, with corresponding upper and lower limits that differ by a factor not exceeding 1 plus 2 divided by p, all within the specified boundary condition context.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a fundamental building block for processing graph-structured data, yet their functionality is often misunderstood, particularly their convolution operation. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how GCNN convolution operates, using the Max-Pooling Graph Convolutional Neural Network (MAX-Pool GCNN) as a model example. It's demonstrated that the Maximum Pooling layer simplifies the network's training process, thereby enabling analytical solutions for its weights. Additionally, the study shows that the Main Signal to Interference plus Noise (ISIN) ratio can be used to derive an optimal filter shape, which is essentially a mathematical match between the filter and the signal, analogous to the matched filter concept in engineering. This work provides valuable insights into GCNNs, particularly their widely used max-pooling variant, and may guide the development of new, more effective graph-structured machine learning models.

A sequence-to-sequence model with a significant reliance on extensive annotated training data has limited utility in scenarios involving low resource availability. This paper introduces a cutting-edge parsing method, EDEN, which incorporates three key components: extensive pre-training on unlabeled data, an innovative self-learning framework that fine-tunes the model using selected predictions, and a dependency decoding head that captures graph relationships. Through experiments on the CoNLL-24 shared task's English and German datasets, EDEN demonstrated exceptional performance, achieving state-of the-art accuracy on English and near-state-of-the-art on German with 97.01% and 90.34% F1 scores respectively, even in the absence of annotated data.

We've conducted a thorough investigation of the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ semileptonic decay process, utilizing both self-consistent light-front quark model (SC-LFQM) and light-front quark model (LFQM) approaches for the $B$ and $D$ mesons. This study enables a direct comparison between the SC-LFQM and LFQM calculations, highlighting their similarities and differences. Notably, the SC-LFQM exhibits greater consistency when modeling the $B\to D$ form factors in comparison to the standard LFQM. Nevertheless, both methods yield identical results for certain key quantities, such as the ratio of the $|f_{+}(0)|/|f_{0}(0)|$ and difference between the form factors at zero-recoil point. Consequently, SC-LFQM and LFQM produce nearly the same predictions for the critical transition form factors and associated transition parameters.

In this investigation, various branes in type IIA string theory are examined in relation to the K-theory of topological spaces.
